Avoiding the next example after you receive help
questions.exp: 文中对比整章不懂与指出分数出现时迷路，具体请求能给帮助者一个位置。

questions.q: 3. What other bravery does the writer mention?
options: The bravery of hiding every question
The bravery of laughing at a sincere question
The bravery of never raising a hand
The bravery of accepting that you may need more practice or an earlier page
questions.exp: 文中说接受“你需要更多练习”或从头一页开始，也需要勇气。

questions.q: 4. What may students who ask for help become later?
options: Less kind, because they forget being stuck
People who waste more time in silent confusion
Kinder helpers, because they remember the feeling of being stuck
People who never trust that understanding is worth discomfort
questions.exp: 文中说他们后来也会成为更善意的帮助者，因为记得卡住的感觉。

junior.title: 📈 Small Progress Still Counts on a Slow Day
junior.content:
Some days the work looks almost still. You study a page and remember little, or you train and your time does not improve, or you try to be kinder and still lose your temper. It is easy, on such a day, to say that nothing counts unless there is a big leap. That story is discouraging, and it is often untrue. Small progress still counts. A slightly clearer sentence, a slightly calmer reply, or one more problem finished carefully is already movement, even if no one else can see it yet.

Slow days have causes. You may be tired, the material may be new, or yesterday’s leap may need time to settle. Growth is not a straight line on a graph. It is more like a tide, with forward inches and pauses. If you only praise yourself after a dramatic success, you will feel poor on most Tuesdays. If you notice the inches, you can stay in the work long enough for a later leap to become possible.

A practical habit is to write one small evidence of progress before you close the book: a word you can now spell, a step you no longer fear, a moment you apologised sooner than last week. Keep the list somewhere ordinary. Read it when the slow feeling arrives. The list is not vanity. It is fuel. It reminds you that the person who is struggling today is the same person who has already moved.

Students who learn to honour small progress become more patient with themselves and with others. They are less likely to quit a worthy effort at the first flat week. Inspiration is not only a sudden fire. It is also the quiet decision to count the next inch, and to begin again tomorrow.
When a friend is having a slow day too, you can share this way of seeing. One kind sentence about a small step may keep both of you in the work a little longer than a demand for a sudden leap.
junior.translation:
有些日子，工作看起来几乎静止。你学了一页却记住很少，或你训练了而成绩并没有提高，或你想更善意却仍然发了脾气。在这样的一天里，人很容易说：除非有一次大的跳跃，否则什么都不算。那个故事让人沮丧，而且常常并不真实。小小的进步仍然算数。一句稍稍更清楚的话，一个稍稍更平静的回答，或又仔细完成的一道题，已经是移动，即使别人还看不见。

缓慢的日子是有原因的。你也许累了，材料也许是新的，或昨天的跳跃需要时间去落定。成长并不是图上的一条直线。它更像潮水，有向前的几寸，也有停顿。如果你只在一次戏剧性的成功之后才赞美自己，你在大多数星期二都会觉得自己很穷。如果你注意到那些寸进，你就可以在工作里停留得足够久，好让后来的一次跳跃成为可能。

一个实际的习惯，是在合上书之前写下一项小小的进步证据：一个你现在能拼写的单词，一个你不再害怕的步骤，一个你比上周更早道歉的时刻。把这份清单放在一个平常的地方。当缓慢的感觉到来时就读它。清单不是虚荣。它是燃料。它提醒你：今天正在挣扎的那个人，也是已经移动过的同一个人。

学会尊重小小进步的学生，会对自己和他人更有耐心。他们不太会在第一个平坦的星期就放弃一项值得的努力。激励不仅仅是突然的火。它也是数清下一寸、并在明天再次开始的安静决定。
当一位朋友也正在过缓慢的一天时，你可以分享这种看法。一句关于小步骤的善意的话，也许比要求一次突然跳跃，更能让你们两个在工作里多停留一会儿。

questions.q: 1. Why does the passage say small progress still counts?
options: Because only a big leap should ever be noticed
Because slow days have no causes
Because a slightly clearer sentence or one careful problem is already movement
Because no one should write down any evidence
questions.exp: 文中说明稍稍更清楚的句子、更平静的回答或仔细完成的一题已经是移动。

questions.q: 2. How does the writer describe growth?
options: As a straight line with no pauses
As more like a tide, with forward inches and pauses
As a graph that only moves on dramatic Tuesdays
As a reason to feel poor after every inch
questions.exp: 文中把成长比作潮水，有向前的几寸，也有停顿，而不是一条直线。

questions.q: 3. What practical habit is suggested before you close the book?
options: Write one small piece of evidence of progress and read the list on slow days
Erase all signs of struggle
Praise yourself only after a huge success
Quit at the first flat week
questions.exp: 文中建议写下一项小小的进步证据，放在平常的地方，缓慢时读它。

questions.q: 4. What do students who honour small progress become?
options: Less patient, and quicker to quit
People who never begin again tomorrow
People who think inspiration is only a sudden fire
More patient, and less likely to quit a worthy effort after a flat week
questions.exp: 文中说他们对自己和他人更有耐心，不太会在第一个平坦的星期就放弃。

junior.title: 🏺 What Buried Objects Can Tell Us About the Past
junior.content:
Maps can show where a city once stood, but they cannot show how a family cooked dinner or what a child played with. For those smaller stories, explorers of history often look under the ground. Archaeologists dig carefully in layers of soil and record every object they find: a broken bowl, a bead, a tool, a seed, or a piece of cloth. Each object is a clue. Together, the clues can rebuild a picture of daily life that no king’s speech ever bothered to write down.

The work is slow on purpose. A site is divided into squares, and the soil is removed a little at a time with small tools, not with a rush that would smash a fragile cup. The position of an object matters as much as the object itself. A cooking pot next to a hearth tells a different story from the same pot thrown into a well. Photographs, drawings and labels keep this information after the earth has been moved. Without the record, a beautiful find can lose most of its meaning.

Science helps the reading. The style of a pot can suggest a period. The type of seed can show what people grew. Burned wood can be tested for a rough date. Animal bones can hint at meals and at the weather of that time. None of these tests is a complete sentence. They are pieces that researchers fit together, and they sometimes change their minds when a new layer appears. That honesty is part of exploration: the past is not a finished puzzle, but a set of traces we learn to question.

Students can practise a little of this thinking in a museum or even in a family kitchen. Ask not only “What is this?” but “Who used it, and what does that tell us?” A spoon, a ticket or an old key can become a tiny excavation. History is not only famous battles. It is also the quiet objects that waited in the ground until someone was patient enough to listen.
junior.translation:
地图可以显示一座城市曾经站在哪里，却不能显示一个家庭如何做晚餐，或一个孩子曾拿什么玩耍。为了那些更小的故事，历史的探索者常常向地下看。考古学家在一层层土壤里小心地挖掘，并记录找到的每件物品：一只破碗，一粒珠子，一件工具，一粒种子，或一块布。每件物品都是一条线索。这些线索合在一起，可以重建一幅日常生活的图画，而那是国王的演说从不屑于写下来的。

这项工作故意很慢。遗址被分成许多方格，土壤用小工具一点点取走，而不是用一阵会砸碎脆弱杯子的匆忙。一件物品的位置，和物品本身同样重要。炉边的一口锅，与被扔进井里的同一口锅，讲述的是不同的故事。照片、图画和标签在泥土被移走之后仍保存这些信息。没有记录，一件美丽的发现也会失去大部分意义。

科学帮助这种阅读。陶器的风格可以暗示一个时期。种子的种类可以显示人们种过什么。烧过的木头可以测出一个大致年代。动物骨头可以暗示餐食，以及那时的天气。这些测试没有一项是完整的句子。它们是研究者拼在一起的碎片，而当新的一层出现时，他们有时会改变想法。那种诚实是探索的一部分：过去不是一幅已经完成的拼图，而是一组我们学着去提问的痕迹。

学生可以在博物馆，甚至在家庭厨房里，练习一点点这种思考。不仅问“这是什么？”，还问“谁用过它，那又告诉了我们什么？”一把勺子、一张票或一把旧钥匙，都可以变成一次小小的发掘。历史不仅仅是著名的战役。它也是那些在地下等待、直到有人足够耐心去倾听的安静物品。

questions.q: 1. Why do explorers of history look under the ground, according to the passage?
options: Because maps already show how a family cooked dinner
Because a king’s speech always describes every child’s toy
To smash fragile cups as quickly as possible
To find clues in ordinary objects that can rebuild a picture of daily life
questions.exp: 文中说地图无法显示日常生活，考古学家通过地下物品的线索重建日常图景。

questions.q: 2. Why does the position of an object matter so much?
options: Because photographs are never used on a site
Because the soil should be removed all at once
Because a pot beside a hearth tells a different story from a pot in a well
Because labels are more important than the object’s place
questions.exp: 文中举例炉边的锅与井里的锅讲述不同故事，位置与物品本身同样重要。

questions.q: 3. How does science help the reading of a site?
options: It gives one complete sentence that never changes
Styles, seeds, burned wood and bones offer pieces that researchers fit together, and sometimes later revise
It proves that the past is a finished puzzle
It shows that dates from wood are always exact to the day
questions.exp: 文中列举陶器风格、种子、烧过的木头和骨头等碎片，并说明新层出现时看法可能改变。

questions.q: 4. What small practice does the writer suggest for students?
options: Treat a spoon, a ticket or an old key as a tiny excavation, asking who used it and what that tells us
Ask only ‘What is this?’ and stop there
Avoid museums and family kitchens
Study only famous battles and ignore quiet objects
questions.exp: 文中建议不仅问是什么，还问谁用过、说明了什么，日常物品也可成为小小发掘。

junior.title: 🧭 How the Compass Changed Long Sea Voyages
junior.content:
For a long time, sailors near the coast could steer by landmarks: a cliff, a lighthouse, or the shape of a bay. Far from land, those signs disappeared. Stars helped on a clear night, but clouds could hide them for days, and a storm could push a ship off its path with no way to know the direction after the rain. The magnetic compass changed this kind of exploration. A small needle, floating or turning on a pin, kept pointing toward the north, even when the sky was dark. With a heading, a voyage could continue with more confidence.

The compass did not arrive suddenly in every harbour. It was improved over many years, and sailors had to learn its limits. Iron on a ship could pull the needle a little to the side. In some parts of the world the magnetic north is not exactly the same as the true north on a map, so careful users made a correction. Rough waves could make a simple bowl of water hard to read, so later compasses were set in a case that could swing and stay level. History is full of tools that needed practice, not only invention.

Once crews trusted the needle, routes grew longer. Merchants could plan to cross open water instead of hugging every shore. Explorers could keep a record of direction and time, then draw better charts when they returned. Islands that had been found by chance could be found again. This was not only a story of adventure. It was also a story of food, news and ideas travelling farther, and of ships taking greater risks when the path seemed clearer than it really was.

Today a phone can show a map and a position in a second, and it is easy to forget the courage of those earlier crossings. Holding a simple compass on a hike is a way to feel a piece of that history in your hand. The needle still points, quietly, as it did for sailors who could not see the shore. Exploration often changes when a tool makes the unknown a little less blind — and people still have to read that tool with care.
junior.translation:
很长时间里，靠近海岸的水手可以靠地标来掌舵：一座悬崖，一座灯塔，或一个海湾的形状。远离陆地时，那些标志就消失了。星星在晴朗的夜里有帮助，但云可以一连几天把它们藏起来，一场风暴也可以把船推离航线，雨后却无从知道方向。磁罗盘改变了这种探索。一根小针，浮着或在钉上转动，即使天空很暗，也一直指向北方。有了航向，一次航行就可以更有信心地继续。

罗盘并不是突然出现在每一个港口的。它在许多年里被改进，水手也必须学习它的限度。船上的铁会把指针稍稍拉向一边。在世界的某些地方，磁北与地图上的真北并不完全相同，所以细心的使用者会做出校正。汹涌的波浪会让一只简单的水碗难以阅读，于是后来的罗盘被放进可以摆动并保持水平的盒子里。历史里充满了不仅需要发明、也需要练习的工具。

一旦船员信任了那根针，航线就变得更长。商人可以计划穿越开阔的水域，而不必紧贴每一处海岸。探索者可以记下方向和时间，回来后再画出更好的海图。曾经偶然发现的岛屿也可以再次被找到。这不仅仅是冒险的故事。它也是食物、消息和想法走得更远的故事，以及当道路看起来比实际更清楚时，船只承担更大风险的故事。

今天一部手机可以在一秒内显示地图和位置，人们很容易忘记那些更早的横渡所需要的勇气。在徒步时拿一只简单的罗盘，是一种让那段历史的一部分留在手里的方式。指针仍然安静地指向，一如那些看不见海岸的水手所见的那样。当一件工具让未知变得不那么盲目时，探索常常就会改变——而人们仍然必须小心地阅读那件工具。

questions.q: 1. What problem did sailors face far from land before the compass?
options: Clouds and storms could hide the sky and push a ship off its path with no clear direction
Landmarks such as cliffs were always visible
Stars never helped on a clear night
A phone already showed every position
questions.exp: 文中说远离陆地时地标消失，阴云可遮住星星，风暴后可能无法知道方向。

questions.q: 2. What limit of the compass did sailors have to learn?
options: The needle never pointed north in the dark
A swinging case always made the tool worse
Practice was unnecessary once the tool was invented
Iron on a ship, and the difference between magnetic north and true north, could pull or shift the reading
questions.exp: 文中提到船上的铁会拉针，磁北与真北并不总是一致，需要校正。

questions.q: 3. How did trusted compasses change routes?
options: Crews hugged every shore more than before
Charts became less useful after every voyage
Merchants and explorers could cross open water, keep records, and find islands again
Food and ideas travelled a shorter distance
questions.exp: 文中说明航线变长，可穿越开阔水域，记录方向并重访岛屿，食物与想法也走得更远。

questions.q: 4. What does the writer suggest we can still do today?
options: Forget earlier crossings completely
Hold a simple compass on a hike, and remember that a tool still has to be read with care
Throw away every needle because phones are perfect
Use a compass only when the shore is already in sight
questions.exp: 文中建议徒步时拿一只简单罗盘感受这段历史，并提醒仍须小心阅读工具。

junior.title: 📓 Why Explorers Wrote Diaries on the Road
junior.content:
When we think of exploration, we often picture a ship, a desert, or a mountain. We picture less often a notebook that had to be kept dry. Many explorers wrote diaries on the road: the weather, the distance, the plants, the people they met, and the mistakes that almost ended the journey. These pages were not only private feelings. They were a way to remember a path so that others could follow, or avoid, the same route. Without the diaries, a brave crossing could vanish into a story with no map and no dates.

A good field diary is regular and honest. Writers noted the date and the place, even on tired evenings. They described a river’s width, a strange bird, or the taste of an unknown fruit — and they also wrote when they were lost, hungry or wrong. Later readers can learn as much from those hard days as from the successful ones. Drawings of a coastline or a leaf could help when words were not enough. Some diaries were later turned into books that invited more people to care about a distant place.

The habit also protected the truth from memory’s soft changes. After a long voyage, the mind may make a storm smaller or a discovery larger. A page written the same night keeps the first facts. Scientists and map-makers still use this idea: write it down while it is fresh. Historians, in turn, treat old diaries as treasures, but they also ask questions. Was the writer fair to the people who already lived on that land? Did the diary leave anyone out? Exploration records can be rich and also incomplete.

Students can borrow the method on a smaller journey: a hike, a family trip, or a week of watching a tree. A few lines each day — what you saw, what surprised you, what you would do differently — can become a personal history. Years later the notebook will show you not only the place, but the person you were when you first explored it. The bravest tool in a bag is sometimes a pen that does not stop when the day is difficult.
junior.translation:
当我们想到探索，常常会想象一艘船、一片沙漠或一座山。我们较少想象一本必须保持干燥的笔记本。许多探索者在路上写日记：天气，距离，植物，遇见的人，以及那些几乎结束旅程的错误。这些页面不仅仅是私人的感情。它们是记住一条路的方法，好让别人可以跟随，或避开，同一条路线。没有这些日记，一次勇敢的穿越可能消失在一个没有地图、也没有日期的故事里。

一本好的野外日记是规律而诚实的。写的人即使在疲惫的晚上也会记下日期和地点。他们描述一条河的宽度、一只奇怪的鸟，或一种未知水果的味道——他们也会写到自己迷路、饥饿或犯错的时候。后来的读者可以从那些艰难的日子里学到的，和从成功的日子里一样多。海岸线或一片叶子的图画，可以在词语不够用时提供帮助。有些日记后来变成了书，邀请更多人去关心一个遥远的地方。

这种习惯也能保护真相，使它不被记忆柔软的改变所改写。一次长途航行之后，头脑可能把风暴变小，或把发现变大。当天晚上写下的一页会留住最初的事实。科学家和地图绘制者仍然使用这个想法：趁新鲜时写下来。历史学家则把旧日记当作珍宝，但他们也会提问。写的人对已经住在那片土地上的人公平吗？日记有没有把谁漏掉？探索的记录可以很丰富，也可以不完整。

学生可以在一次更小的旅程上借用这种方法：一次徒步，一次家庭旅行，或一周观察一棵树。每天几行——你看见了什么，什么让你吃惊，你会把什么做得不同——可以成为一段个人的历史。多年以后，这本笔记本会让你看见的，不仅是那个地方，还有你第一次探索它时的自己。行囊里最勇敢的工具，有时是一支在日子艰难时也不停下的笔。

questions.q: 1. Why were explorers’ diaries more than private feelings?
options: Because a brave crossing needs no map and no dates
Because they helped later people follow or avoid the same route, with dates and details
Because notebooks were never kept dry
Because drawings were forbidden on the road
questions.exp: 文中说日记是记住道路的方法，好让别人跟随或避开同一路线，没有日记，穿越可能变成没有地图和日期的故事。

questions.q: 2. What makes a good field diary, according to the passage?
options: Being regular and honest, with dates, places, hard days, and drawings when words are not enough
Writing only on successful days and hiding hunger
Waiting until memory has made the storm smaller
Leaving out anything that later becomes a book
questions.exp: 文中强调规律而诚实，记下日期地点，也写下迷路与饥饿，并可用图画补充。

questions.q: 3. Why do historians still ask questions about old diaries?
options: Because diaries are never useful as treasures
Because scientists refuse to write anything down while it is fresh
Because the first facts on a same-night page cannot be trusted
Because a record can be rich and still incomplete, and may be unfair to people who already lived there
questions.exp: 文中说历史学家把日记当珍宝，也会问写的人是否公平、是否漏掉了谁，记录可能不完整。

questions.q: 4. How can students borrow this method?
options: Only by crossing a desert with a famous crew
By stopping the pen whenever the day is difficult
By writing a few lines each day on a hike or a small trip, so the notebook later shows both the place and the person they were
By never watching a tree or taking a family trip
questions.exp: 文中建议在徒步、家庭旅行或观察一棵树时每天写几行，多年后可见地方与当时的自己。

junior.title: 🪁 Traditional Games That Children Still Play
junior.content:
Not every sport begins in a huge stadium. Long before modern teams and tickets, children played games with what they had: a rope, a stone, a stick, a shuttlecock, or a song that told them when to run. Many of those traditional games are still alive in schoolyards and parks. They are a kind of culture you can feel in your legs and your laughter, not only in a museum. When a grandparent teaches a game from their own childhood, a piece of local history jumps a generation in one afternoon.

These games often look simple, yet they train the body and the mind. Hopping on one foot, skipping a rope, or keeping a feathered shuttlecock in the air needs balance, timing and attention. A circle game that sends a child in and out of the group also teaches waiting, fairness and quick thinking. Rules can change a little from street to street, and that is part of their charm. Children learn to agree on a rule before they start, which is a small lesson in living together.

Around the world the same idea wears different clothes. One place may love a kicking game in a narrow alley. Another may play a clapping rhyme or a tug of war at a festival. When families move, they sometimes carry a game with them, and the schoolyard becomes a meeting of styles. A child who learns both the new game and the old one holds two cultures at once. Sports days can make room for these games beside the usual races, so that winning is not the only story.

You do not need expensive equipment to join this history. A piece of chalk, a rubber band, or an open patch of ground can be enough. Ask an older relative which game they remember, try it with friends, and then teach it again. Culture is not only something we watch on a screen. Sometimes it is a familiar rhyme, a shared rule, and the happy tiredness after play.
junior.translation:
并非每项运动都始于一座巨大的体育场。在现代的球队和门票出现之前很久，孩子们就用他们拥有的东西做游戏：一根绳子，一块石头，一根棍子，一个毽子，或一首告诉他们何时跑起来的歌。这些传统游戏里，仍有许多活在校园和公园里。它们是一种你可以在腿上和笑声里感觉到的文化，而不仅仅存在于博物馆中。当一位祖父母把他们童年的游戏教出来时，一块地方历史就在一个下午跳过了一代人。

这些游戏常常看起来简单，却在训练身体和头脑。单脚跳、跳绳，或让一个带羽毛的毽子不落地，都需要平衡、时机和注意力。一个让孩子进出圈子的圆圈游戏，也在教等待、公平和快速思考。规则可以从一条街到另一条街稍有不同，而这正是它们的魅力的一部分。孩子们在开始之前学习商定规则，这是关于一起生活的一小课。

在世界各地，同一个想法穿着不同的衣服。一个地方可能喜欢在窄巷里做踢球的游戏。另一个地方可能在节日里玩拍手歌谣或拔河。当家庭迁移时，他们有时会把一种游戏带走，于是校园就成了风格的会面处。一个既学会新游戏、又保留旧游戏的孩子，便同时握着两种文化。运动日可以在通常的赛跑旁边为这些游戏留出位置，好让获胜不是唯一的故事。

你不需要昂贵的装备来加入这段历史。一根粉笔，一根橡皮筋，或一小块空地就足够了。问问年长的亲戚他们记得哪一种游戏，和朋友一起试试，然后再把它教出去。文化不仅仅是我们在屏幕上观看的东西。有时它是一首熟悉的歌谣，一条共享的规则，以及玩过之后那份愉快的疲倦。

questions.q: 1. Why does the passage call traditional games a kind of culture?
options: Because they can only be felt in a museum, never in a park
Because every sport must begin in a huge stadium
Because they are felt in play, and a grandparent’s game can pass local history in one afternoon
Because children never used ropes, stones or songs
questions.exp: 文中说这些游戏可以在腿和笑声里感觉到，祖父母的传授能让地方历史跳过一代。

questions.q: 2. What do these simple games train besides the body?
options: Only the ability to ignore rules
Balance and timing, and also waiting, fairness and agreeing on a rule before starting
A habit of never changing a rule from street to street
The wish to make winning the only story
questions.exp: 文中提到平衡、时机、注意力，以及等待、公平和开始前商定规则。

questions.q: 3. What can happen when families move and carry a game with them?
options: The schoolyard can become a meeting of styles, and a child may hold two cultures at once
All old games must disappear at once
Sports days must ban every traditional game
Only one alley game is allowed in the world
questions.exp: 文中说校园成为风格的会面处，学会新旧两种游戏的孩子同时握着两种文化。

questions.q: 4. What does the writer say you need in order to join this history?
options: Expensive equipment and a huge stadium ticket
A screen that plays the rhyme for you so you never try it
A rule that friends must not play together
Simple things such as chalk, a rubber band or an open patch of ground, plus asking and teaching the game
questions.exp: 文中说不需要昂贵装备，粉笔、橡皮筋或空地就够，并建议向亲戚请教再教给别人。

junior.title: 🎽 Why Sports Fans Wear Colours and Sing Together
junior.content:
A sports match is not only the players on the field. Around them sits a second performance: the fans. They wear the same colours, wave flags, and sing songs that everyone in the group seems to know. To a visitor this can look loud and strange. To the people inside it, the colours and the singing are a language of belonging. For ninety minutes, or for a whole tournament, strangers can feel like neighbours who share one hope.

This fan culture has roots. A colour may come from a city’s flag, a school’s uniform, or a club’s long history. A song may have been born in one famous season and then taught to children who never saw that team. When the crowd sings, it is repeating a story: we were here, we suffered a loss, we came back. Scarves, painted faces and lucky shirts are small rituals, a bit like festival clothes. They tell the eye, in one second, which community you have joined.

There is a kind of warmth in this, and also a duty. Belonging should not turn into unkindness toward the other side. Real sport culture includes respect for the visiting team and for the referee, and it leaves the stadium without breaking seats or cruel words. Many clubs now ask fans to look after one another, including people who are new and do not yet know the songs. A good crowd is loud in support, and careful in its manners.

Students who join a school team’s stands can feel a piece of this culture in a safer size. Learn the chant, wear the colour if you wish, and also clap for a fair play by either side. Years later you may forget the score, but you may remember the feeling of many voices becoming one. That memory is why fans keep singing: not only to push the team, but to remind themselves that they belong to something larger than a single afternoon.
junior.translation:
一场体育比赛不仅仅是场上的球员。在他们周围，还有第二场表演：球迷。他们穿着同样的颜色，挥舞旗帜，并唱着这一群里似乎人人都知道的歌。对一个来访者来说，这可能显得吵闹而奇怪。对里面的人来说，这些颜色和歌唱是一种归属的语言。在九十分钟里，或在整个锦标赛里，陌生人可以感觉像分享同一个希望的邻居。

这种球迷文化是有根的。一种颜色可能来自一座城市的旗帜、一所学校的校服，或一家俱乐部的长久历史。一首歌可能诞生于某一个著名的赛季，然后被教给从未见过那支队伍的孩子。当人群歌唱时，它是在重复一个故事：我们在这里，我们承受过失败，我们又回来了。围巾、涂画的脸和幸运衬衫是小小的仪式，有一点像节日的衣服。它们在一秒钟内告诉眼睛，你加入了哪一个共同体。

这里面有一种温暖，也有一种责任。归属不应该变成对另一方的不友善。真正的体育文化包括对客队和裁判的尊重，并且在离开体育场时不砸座位，也不留下残忍的话。许多俱乐部现在请球迷彼此照顾，包括那些新来、还不会唱那些歌的人。一个好的观众席在支持时是响亮的，在礼貌上是谨慎的。

加入校队看台的学生，可以在更安全的尺寸里感觉到这种文化的一部分。学会那句呐喊，如果你愿意就穿上那种颜色，并且也为任何一方的一次公平竞技鼓掌。多年以后你也许会忘记比分，但你也许会记得许多声音变成一个声音的感觉。那份记忆就是球迷继续歌唱的原因：不仅是为了推动球队，也是为了提醒自己，他们属于比单独一个下午更巨大的某种东西。

questions.q: 1. What does the passage say the colours and the singing are for the fans?
options: A reason to be unkind to the visiting team
A performance that only the players on the field can see
A rule that visitors must never watch a match
A language of belonging that can make strangers feel like neighbours who share one hope
questions.exp: 文中说颜色和歌唱是归属的语言，陌生人可以感觉像分享同一个希望的邻居。

questions.q: 2. Where can a team’s colour or song come from?
options: Only from a lucky shirt with no history
From a plan to break seats after the match
From a city’s flag, a school’s uniform, or a famous season later taught to children
From a story that must never be repeated
questions.exp: 文中指出颜色可能来自城市旗帜、校服或俱乐部历史，歌曲可能来自著名赛季并传给孩子。

questions.q: 3. What duty comes with this kind of belonging?
options: A duty to use cruel words if your side is losing
Respect for the visiting team and the referee, and careful manners in the stadium
A duty to keep new fans from learning the songs
A duty to forget support and stay silent
questions.exp: 文中强调归属不应变成不友善，应尊重客队与裁判，离开时不破坏、不说残忍的话。

questions.q: 4. What may students remember years later from the school stands?
options: The feeling of many voices becoming one, and of belonging to something larger than a single afternoon
Only the exact score of every match
That clapping for fair play is never allowed
That colours must never be worn at school
questions.exp: 文中说多年后也许会忘记比分，但会记得许多声音合成一个的感觉，以及属于更巨大事物的提醒。

junior.title: 🤝 Fair Play: The Hidden Culture Inside a Match
junior.content:
People often talk about speed, strength and winning when they talk about sport. There is another culture inside every good match, and it is quieter: fair play. Fair play means you follow the rules when no official is looking, you accept a decision you dislike, and you treat the other team as opponents, not as enemies. A handshake before or after the game, a hand offered to a fallen player, and an honest “it was out” are small scenes that teach more than a trophy can.

This culture has to be practised, because the wish to win is strong. A child may be tempted to hide a handball, or to cheer when someone is hurt. Coaches and parents shape the lesson in those seconds. If the adults only praise the score, the hidden culture grows weak. If they also praise a truthful word and a calm response, the players learn that character is part of the sport. Referees deserve this culture too. Arguing without respect turns a game into a quarrel, and younger children copy what they see.

Fair play is not the same as being soft. You can still run hard, try a clever move, and care about the result. The line is this: you do not cheat, and you do not try to harm. Many tournaments now give a fair-play award besides the first-place cup, which is a public way of saying that how you win matters. Supporters can join the culture by refusing cruel chants. A match is a public class in how a community handles competition.

Students can carry the same idea into class games and even into board games at home. Keep the rule you agreed on. Admit a mistake. Congratulate the other side when they play well. These habits look small, but they travel with you into later teams, later jobs, and later arguments. The hidden culture of fair play is one of sport’s best gifts, because it can still guide you when the stadium lights are off.
junior.translation:
人们谈体育时，常常谈到速度、力量和获胜。每一场好的比赛里面，还有另一种更安静的文化：公平竞赛。公平竞赛意味着在没有裁判注意时你也遵守规则，你接受一个你不喜欢的判罚，并且把另一队当作对手，而不是敌人。赛前或赛后的一次握手，向跌倒的球员伸出的一只手，以及一句诚实的“出界了”，都是比奖杯更能教导人的小场面。

这种文化必须被练习，因为求胜的愿望很强。一个孩子可能会想要隐瞒一次手球，或在有人受伤时欢呼。教练和父母在那些秒里塑造这一课。如果成年人只赞美比分，这种隐藏的文化就会变弱。如果他们也赞美一句诚实的话和一次冷静的回应，球员就会学到品格是这项运动的一部分。裁判也值得拥有这种文化。没有尊重的争辩会把比赛变成争吵，而更小的孩子会模仿他们所看见的。

公平竞赛并不等于软弱。你仍然可以奋力奔跑，尝试一次巧妙的动作，并在乎结果。那条界线是：你不作弊，也不企图伤害。许多锦标赛现在除了冠军杯之外，还会颁发公平竞赛奖，这是一种公开的方式，用来说明你如何获胜是重要的。支持者也可以加入这种文化，拒绝残忍的呐喊。一场比赛是一个共同体如何对待竞争的公开课堂。

学生可以把同样的想法带进课堂游戏，甚至带进家里的棋类游戏。遵守你们商定的规则。承认错误。当对方打得好时向他们祝贺。这些习惯看起来很小，但它们会跟着你走进后来的队伍、后来的工作和后来的争论。公平竞赛这种隐藏的文化，是体育最好的礼物之一，因为当体育场的灯关掉以后，它仍然可以指引你。

questions.q: 1. What does fair play mean in the passage?
options: Following the rules even when no official is looking, accepting hard decisions, and treating the other team as opponents, not enemies
Hiding a handball in order to win
Cheering when someone is hurt
Treating the referee as an enemy in every match
questions.exp: 文中把公平竞赛定义为无人注意时也守规则、接受不喜欢的判罚、把对方当对手而非敌人。

questions.q: 2. How can adults weaken or strengthen this hidden culture?
options: By never speaking to coaches or parents
By arguing without respect so that younger children can copy it
By cancelling every handshake after the game
By praising only the score, or by also praising a truthful word and a calm response
questions.exp: 文中说若只赞美比分，隐藏文化会变弱；若也赞美诚实与冷静，球员会学到品格是运动的一部分。

questions.q: 3. Why do some tournaments give a fair-play award?
options: To prove that fair play is the same as being soft
To encourage cruel chants from supporters
As a public way of saying that how you win matters, not only who is first
To show that cheating is allowed if you run hard
questions.exp: 文中说明公平竞赛奖是一种公开表达：你如何获胜是重要的。

questions.q: 4. How can students carry fair play beyond the stadium?
options: By forgetting these habits after the lights go off
By keeping agreed rules, admitting mistakes, and congratulating the other side in class or home games
By using one set of rules only when an official is watching
By refusing to play any board game at home
questions.exp: 文中建议把守约、认错和祝贺带进课堂游戏和家里的棋类游戏，这些习惯会走进后来的工作与争论。

junior.title: 🏛️ How Old Buildings Tell the Story of a Town
junior.content:
A town’s history is not only in books. It is also in walls, roofs and doorways that have stood through many winters. An old building can tell you what people once needed: a wide gate for carts, a thick wall for safety, a courtyard for shared work, or high windows to catch the light. If you walk slowly and look up, the street becomes a classroom. Stone, brick and wood keep a memory of tools, tastes and money from times that no longer speak.

The details matter. A faded shop sign may show a trade that has disappeared. A row of similar houses may show a period when many families arrived at once. Carvings above a door, a family name, or a date in iron can mark a proud year. Even a repair is a sentence in the story: a modern roof on an old room says that someone chose to stay and continue, not to tear everything down. When a building is lost, a piece of that local language goes with it, which is why some towns work hard to protect a hall, a bridge or a small temple.

Old buildings also hold mixed feelings. They may be beautiful and also inconvenient. They may remind one group of a happy past and another group of a hard one. Culture and history meet in that argument: what should we keep, what may we change, and how can a new use — a library in an old warehouse, a café in an old station — keep the walls alive for people today? A living building is often a better teacher than an empty one that no one may enter.

Students can practise reading a street near home. Choose one old building, sketch it, and ask an older neighbour what it used to be. Look for a date, a material, or a shape that feels different from the new flats nearby. Then write a short paragraph as if the building could talk. You will be doing a kind of history work: listening to the quiet culture that still stands at the corner, waiting to be noticed.
junior.translation:
一座城镇的历史不仅仅在书里。它也在那些度过许多冬天的墙壁、屋顶和门道里。一座旧建筑可以告诉你人们曾经需要什么：供马车进出的宽门，为了安全的厚墙，供共同劳动的庭院，或为了采光的高窗。如果你慢慢走并抬起头来，街道就变成一间教室。石头、砖和木头保存着关于工具、趣味和金钱的记忆，而来自那些已经不再说话的时代。

细节很重要。一块褪色的店招可能显示一种已经消失的行业。一排相似的房屋可能显示许多家庭同时到来的一个时期。门上的雕刻、一个家族的姓，或铁里的一个日期，可以标记一个骄傲的年份。即使一次修缮也是故事里的一句话：旧房间上的新屋顶表明有人选择留下并继续，而不是把一切拆掉。当一座建筑消失时，这种地方语言的一块也会随之而去，这就是为什么有些城镇努力保护一座厅堂、一座桥或一座小庙。

旧建筑也装着复杂的感情。它们可能美丽，也可能不方便。它们可能让一群人想起快乐的过去，却让另一群人想起艰难的过去。文化与历史在那场争论里相遇：什么该保留，什么可以改变，以及一种新的用途——旧仓库里的图书馆，旧车站里的咖啡馆——如何能让这些墙为今天的人继续活着？一座被使用的建筑，常常比一座无人可进的空房子是更好的老师。

学生可以练习阅读家附近的一条街。选一座旧建筑，画下它，并问一位年长的邻居它曾经是什么。寻找一个日期、一种材料，或一种与附近新公寓不同的形状。然后写一小段，就好像这座建筑会说话。你将会在做一种历史工作：倾听那种仍然站在街角、等待被注意的安静文化。

questions.q: 1. What can an old building tell you, according to the passage?
options: Only the names in a history book, never what people once needed
What people once needed, such as a wide gate, a thick wall, a courtyard or high windows
That stone and wood keep no memory at all
That you should never look up while walking
questions.exp: 文中说旧建筑可以告诉人们曾经需要什么，并举例宽门、厚墙、庭院和高窗。

questions.q: 2. Why can even a repair be part of the story?
options: Because a modern roof on an old room can show that someone chose to stay and continue
Because every repair means the town must tear the building down
Because faded shop signs should be ignored
Because dates in iron never mark a year
questions.exp: 文中把修缮也看作故事中的句子：新屋顶说明有人选择留下并继续，而不是全部拆掉。

questions.q: 3. How can a new use keep old walls alive?
options: By locking the building so that no one may enter
By refusing to discuss what we keep or change
By making every old building only inconvenient and never useful
By giving the place a new job, such as a library in an old warehouse or a café in an old station
questions.exp: 文中举例旧仓库改图书馆、旧车站改咖啡馆，让墙为今天的人继续活着。

questions.q: 4. What street-reading task is suggested for students?
options: Photograph only new flats and ignore all dates and materials
Avoid older neighbours and never write a paragraph
Choose one old building, sketch it, ask a neighbour what it used to be, and write as if it could talk
Study only famous battles, never a corner building
questions.exp: 文中建议选一座旧建筑来画、向邻居打听、寻找日期或材料，并写一段让建筑说话。

junior.title: 🔔 How Town Bells Once Shared News With Everyone
junior.content:
Before phones and loudspeakers, many towns had a voice that everyone could hear: a bell. High in a tower, the bell marked the hours, called people to a meeting, or warned them of fire and flood. Different patterns of ringing could mean different things, and people learned those patterns the way we now learn a ringtone. Culture and history lived in the sound. You did not need to be able to read a notice to know that something important was happening in the shared air.

The bell shaped daily life. Farmers in nearby fields could tell when to come home. Markets could open and close with a ring. A funeral, a wedding, or a festival might have its own music from the same tower. In this way one instrument served many chapters of a community’s story. Someone had to climb the stairs and do the work in every kind of weather, so the bell was also a job and a duty, not only a pretty sound. When travellers arrived, the familiar tone could tell them they were close to a known place.

Times changed, and many of these jobs moved to clocks, radios and phones. Some bells fell silent; others are kept for ceremonies or for a weekly hour that reminds a city of its older self. Arguments appear, too: a morning ring may comfort one neighbour and wake another who needs rest. That debate is also history in motion — a town deciding how much of its old sound should remain in a busier, more private age.

If you walk past a tower, pause and ask when the bell still rings, and why. Visit on a festival day if you can, and listen with the crowd. You may not understand every pattern, but you will hear a piece of the way people once shared news: not one message to one person, but one sound to all. Remembering that public voice helps us see how culture travelled through a town, long before a screen lit up in someone’s hand.
junior.translation:
在电话和喇叭之前，许多城镇有一个人人都能听见的声音：一口钟。在高高的塔上，钟标记着钟点，召唤人们去开会，或警告他们火灾和洪水。不同的敲法可以表示不同的事情，人们学习那些节奏，就像我们现在学习铃声。文化和历史活在这声音里。你不必会读一张告示，也能知道共享的空气里正发生着重要的事。

钟塑造了日常生活。附近田里的农夫可以知道何时回家。市场可以随着一声敲响而开张和关闭。葬礼、婚礼或节日，可能从同一座塔里发出各自的音乐。就这样，一件乐器服务着一个共同体故事里的许多章节。必须有人在每一种天气里爬上楼梯去做这项工作，所以钟也是一份工作和一种责任，而不仅仅是好听的声音。当旅行者到来时，那熟悉的音色可以告诉他们，自己已经接近一个认识的地方。

时代变了，这些工作里有许多搬到了时钟、广播和电话上。有些钟沉寂了；另一些被留给仪式，或留给一个提醒城市想起更老的自己的每周时辰。争论也会出现：早晨的一声也许安慰一位邻居，却吵醒另一位需要休息的人。那场辩论也是正在进行的历史——一座城镇在决定，在一个更忙碌、也更私人的时代里，该留下多少旧日的声音。

如果你走过一座塔，停下来问问钟如今何时还敲，以及为什么。如果可以，就在节日里和人群一起听。你也许不能理解每一种节奏，但你会听到人们曾经分享消息的一种方式：不是一条送给一个人的信息，而是一声送给所有人的声音。记住那公共的嗓音，能帮助我们看见文化在屏幕在某个人手里亮起之前，是如何穿过一座城镇的。

questions.q: 1. What jobs could a town bell do before phones, according to the passage?
options: It could send a private message to only one person
It could replace every festival with a silent tower
It could mark the hours, call a meeting, or warn people of fire and flood
It could teach people to ignore shared sounds
questions.exp: 文中说钟标记钟点、召唤开会，或警告火灾和洪水。

questions.q: 2. How did the bell shape daily life?
options: It had no link to markets, fields or ceremonies
Farmers, markets, funerals and weddings could all be guided by the same tower, and someone had to ring it as a duty
Travellers could never recognise a familiar tone
The bell was only decoration and never a job
questions.exp: 文中举例农夫回家、市场开闭、婚丧节日的不同敲法，并指出有人必须爬塔履行责任。

questions.q: 3. Why do arguments about ringing still appear today?
options: Because a morning ring may comfort one neighbour and wake another, and the town must decide how much old sound to keep
Because every bell has already fallen silent forever
Because radios never took over any of the old jobs
Because ceremonies cannot use a bell any longer
questions.exp: 文中谈到早晨的钟可能安慰一人、吵醒另一人，城镇需决定在更私人的时代留下多少旧声音。

questions.q: 4. What does the writer want you to remember when you listen?
options: That a screen in the hand is the only way culture ever travelled
That you must understand every pattern before you may pause
That public voices never mattered in a town’s history
That news was once one sound to all, not only one message to one person
questions.exp: 文中说那是一声送给所有人的声音，记住这公共嗓音有助于理解文化如何穿过城镇。

junior.title: 👘 What Old Clothes Can Teach Us About Daily History
junior.content:
History is often told through palaces and battles, but daily culture also hides in clothes. A heavy coat, a wide hat, a work apron, or a pair of cloth shoes can show what the weather was like, what work people did, and what a community thought was proper or beautiful. Museums sometimes display a wedding dress or a uniform as if it were only pretty. If you look more closely, the stitches, the patches and the material are records: time spent, money saved, and skills passed from one pair of hands to another.

Clothes also mark change. When factories began to make fabric more cheaply, more families could own a second set of garments, and colours that had once been rare appeared in ordinary streets. New jobs asked for new pockets, stronger boots, or safer hats. Travel mixed styles: a button, a pattern or a way of folding a cloth could arrive from far away and then feel local after a generation. Even a school uniform is a small historical document. It tells you what a society wanted students to look like, and how that idea has shifted.

There is care in this kind of history. Some old clothes were made for people who had little choice about what they wore. Some fashions were unfair to the workers who produced them. Looking at a beautiful robe should include asking who sewed it and how long the day was. Culture is richer when we see both the celebration and the labour. Families can join this work by keeping one well-loved item and the story that belongs to it, rather than throwing every worn shirt away without a word.

Students can try a simple study at home. Choose a piece of clothing from an older relative, ask when it was worn, and write down what it was for — work, a festival, a cold winter, or a special photograph. If possible, notice the repair. A patch is evidence that someone valued the cloth enough to keep it alive. Daily history is not distant. Sometimes it hangs in a cupboard, smelling faintly of soap and time, ready to teach if we ask.
junior.translation:
历史常常通过宫殿和战役来讲述，但日常文化也藏在衣服里。一件厚外套，一顶宽帽，一条工作围裙，或一双布鞋，都可以显示当时的天气如何，人们做什么工作，以及一个共同体认为什么是得体的或美丽的。博物馆有时把一件婚纱或一套制服陈列得仿佛只是好看。如果你看得更近，针脚、补丁和材料都是记录：花去的时间，省下的钱，以及从一双手传到另一双手的技能。

衣服也标记着变化。当工厂开始更便宜地生产布料时，更多家庭能够拥有第二套衣服，一度稀少的颜色也出现在平常的街道上。新的工作要求新的口袋、更结实的靴子，或更安全的帽子。旅行混合了风格：一粒纽扣、一种图案或一种叠布的方法，可以从远方到来，并在一代人之后变得本地。即使一套校服也是一份小小的历史文件。它告诉你一个社会希望学生看起来怎样，以及那个想法如何已经转变。

这种历史里也有需要小心对待的地方。有些旧衣服是为那些对穿着几乎没有选择的人做的。有些时尚对生产它们的工人并不公平。看着一件美丽的袍子，也应该问问是谁缝的，那一天有多长。当我们既看见庆祝、也看见劳动时，文化会更丰富。家庭可以加入这项工作，留下一件被好好爱过的衣物和属于它的故事，而不是不说一句话就把每一件旧衬衫扔掉。

学生可以在家里试一次简单的研究。从一位年长的亲戚那里选一件衣服，问问它是何时穿的，并写下它是做什么用的——工作，一个节日，一个寒冷的冬天，或一张特别的照片。如果可能，注意那些修理。一块补丁是证据，说明有人足够珍惜这块布，才让它继续活着。日常的历史并不遥远。有时它就挂在橱柜里，带着一点肥皂和时间的气味，如果我们开口问，它就愿意教学。

questions.q: 1. What can ordinary clothes show about daily history?
options: Only the story of palaces and battles
That stitches and patches have no meaning
That museums should display dresses only as pretty objects
The weather, the work people did, and what a community thought was proper or beautiful
questions.exp: 文中说厚外套、围裙或布鞋可以显示天气、工作和共同体对得体与美丽的看法。

questions.q: 2. How did cheaper factory fabric change daily life?
options: Fewer families could own a second set of garments
Travel stopped mixing styles after one generation
More families could own extra clothes, new colours appeared, and new jobs asked for new kinds of pockets and boots
School uniforms stopped being historical documents
questions.exp: 文中说明更多家庭能拥有第二套衣服，稀少颜色进入街道，新工作带来新口袋与靴子。

questions.q: 3. What careful question should we ask when we look at a beautiful robe?
options: Whether we can throw every worn shirt away without a story
Who sewed it and how long the day was, so that labour is seen beside celebration
Whether fashions are always fair to workers automatically
Whether families must never keep a well-loved item
questions.exp: 文中提醒看着美丽袍子时也应问是谁缝的、工作日有多长，文化应同时看见庆祝与劳动。

questions.q: 4. What home study does the writer suggest?
options: Choose a relative’s garment, ask when it was worn and what it was for, and notice a patch as evidence of care
Ignore repairs and never talk to older relatives
Study only new clothes that have no history
Write nothing down about festivals, winters or photographs
questions.exp: 文中建议选一件亲戚的衣服，询问穿着时间与用途，并注意补丁作为被珍惜的证据。

junior.title: 📅 Planning the Week on Sunday Evening
junior.content:
Time is easier to manage when you can see a whole week, not only tonight’s homework. A short Sunday-evening plan can turn a foggy Monday into a clearer road. Sit down with a simple calendar or a notebook page divided into seven days. Write the fixed things first: school hours, a lesson, a family dinner, a match. Then place the bigger pieces of homework and the chores that always surprise you on Wednesday night. The aim is not to fill every square. The aim is to see where the busy days already are, and to give hard work a home before it arrives in a rush.

The plan should be kind and honest. If a project needs three evenings, do not pretend it needs one. Leave a little empty space for a delay, a longer assignment, or a rest that you will actually need. Put a short review on a quieter afternoon rather than on the night before a test. When two events collide, choose on Sunday, not in a panic at the gate. A good weekly picture also shows your sleep and your meals, because a timetable that ignores the body will not survive until Friday.

This habit works best when you look at the plan once each afternoon and adjust it with a pencil. The week will not obey every line, and that is normal. Crossing out and moving a task is still time management; it is the map being updated. Families can help by sharing the big dates, so that a visit or a repair does not appear from nowhere. Students who do this often feel less hunted, because they have already met the week once in a calm hour.

At the end of Sunday, close the notebook and let the evening be an evening. The plan is a tool, not a master. If you keep this appointment with yourself for a month, you will learn the real shape of your days: which subjects need more room, and which tasks can wait. Managing time begins with seeing it, and Sunday is a quiet place to look.
junior.translation:
当你能看见整整一周，而不只是今晚的作业时，时间会更好管理。一段简短的周日晚上的计划，可以把雾蒙蒙的星期一变成更清楚的路。坐下来，用一个简单的日历，或一页分成七天的笔记本。先写下固定的事情：上课的时间，一节课，一次家庭晚餐，一场比赛。然后把较大的作业，以及总在周三晚上突然出现的家务，放进格子里。目的不是填满每一个方格。目的是看见哪些日子已经很忙，并在困难的工作匆忙到来之前，先给它一个家。

计划应当既善意又诚实。如果一个项目需要三个晚上，就不要假装它只需要一个。留一点空位给延误、更长的作业，或你真正会需要的休息。把一次短复习放在更安静的下午，而不是考试前的那个夜里。当两件事撞在一起时，在星期天选择，而不是在校门口惊慌地选择。一幅好的每周图画也会显示你的睡眠和膳食，因为一份忽略身体的时间表，是活不到星期五的。

这个习惯在你每天下午看一次计划、并用铅笔调整时，效果最好。这一周不会服从每一条线，那是正常的。划掉并移动一项任务，仍然是时间管理；那是地图正在被更新。家庭可以通过分享重要日期来帮忙，好让一次拜访或一次修理不会从别处突然冒出来。常常这样做的学生会较少有被追赶的感觉，因为他们已经在一个平静的小时里见过这一周一次了。

在星期天结束时，合上笔记本，让这个晚上仍然是一个晚上。计划是工具，不是主人。如果你对自己遵守这个约定一个月，你就会学到自己日子的真正形状：哪些科目需要更多空间，哪些任务可以等待。管理时间从看见时间开始，而星期天是一个安静的观看之处。

questions.q: 1. What should you write first on a Sunday-evening plan?
options: The fixed things first, such as school hours, a lesson, a family dinner or a match
Only the chores that surprise you on Wednesday
Every square of the week, with no empty space
Only tonight’s homework and nothing else
questions.exp: 文中建议先写下固定的事情：上课时间、课、家庭晚餐、比赛，再放大作业和家务。

questions.q: 2. Why should the plan leave a little empty space?
options: Because sleep and meals should never appear on a timetable
So that two events can collide at the school gate
Because a project that needs three evenings should be written as one
For a delay, a longer assignment, or a rest you will actually need
questions.exp: 文中说留一点空位给延误、更长的作业或真正需要的休息，忽略身体的时间表活不到周五。

questions.q: 3. What is still time management when the week does not obey the plan?
options: Throwing the notebook away
Refusing to share big dates with the family
Crossing out and moving a task, as if updating a map, after a calm daily look
Never adjusting the lines with a pencil
questions.exp: 文中说划掉并移动任务仍然是时间管理，是地图在更新。

questions.q: 4. What can you learn if you keep the Sunday habit for a month?
options: That the plan must become a master of the evening
The real shape of your days: which subjects need more room, and which tasks can wait
That Sunday should be filled with panic
That seeing time is unnecessary for managing it
questions.exp: 文中说坚持一个月会学到日子的真正形状：哪些科目需要更多空间，哪些任务可以等待。

junior.title: 📏 Learning How Long a Task Really Takes
junior.content:
Many time plans fail for a simple reason: the work takes longer than we guessed. A student writes “finish the report” in a thirty-minute box, then discovers that finding the title page, checking the figures and making a neat copy need a whole evening. The problem is not only laziness. The problem is a weak sense of how long a task really takes. Time management improves when you become a better estimator, the way a cook becomes better at knowing when the rice is done.

You can train this sense with a notebook. Before you start, write down your guess in minutes. When you finish, write the real time. After a week you will see a pattern. Reading a chapter may be close to your guess, while writing and rewriting may be twice as long. Packing a school bag may be quick on a calm morning and slow when you cannot find a book. These notes are not meant to shame you. They are data. The next plan can give writing a wider box, and can place a short search for missing things before you leave.

People often forget the hidden minutes around a task: opening the files, sharpening a pencil, walking to the library, or waiting for a page to print. If you count only the “main work,” the edges will steal the hour. A fair estimate includes those edges, and also a little extra for a hard paragraph. When a task is new, double the first guess and see what happens. Being a little early is kinder than being late and rushed.

Families and classmates can share their honest times without competing. Knowing that a poster usually takes two evenings helps everyone plan. Students who measure their work start fewer fights with the clock, because the clock is no longer a surprise. The skill looks ordinary, yet it is one of the most useful in later study and later jobs. To manage time, you must first tell the truth about time — including the time you did not see at the start.
junior.translation:
许多时间计划失败，是因为一个简单的原因：工作比我们猜测的更久。一个学生在三十分钟的格子里写下“完成报告”，然后发现找标题页、核对数字和抄写工整需要整整一个晚上。问题不仅仅是懒惰。问题是对一项任务真正需要多久缺少感觉。当你成为一个更好的估计者时，时间管理就会改善，就像厨师更善于知道米饭何时熟了一样。

你可以用一个笔记本训练这种感觉。开始之前，写下你以分钟计的猜测。结束时，写下真实的时间。一周之后你会看见一种模式。读一章也许接近你的猜测，而写作和重写也许要两倍久。在平静的早晨收拾书包也许很快，而当你找不到一本书时就会很慢。这些笔记不是为了让你羞愧。它们是数据。下一次计划可以给写作一个更宽的格子，并在出门前安排一段寻找缺失物品的短时间。

人们常常忘记一项任务周围那些隐藏的分钟：打开文件，削一支铅笔，走到图书馆，或等一页纸打印出来。如果你只计算“主要工作”，边缘就会偷走这个小时。一个公平的估计包括那些边缘，也为困难的一段留一点额外时间。当任务是新的时，把第一次猜测加倍，再看看会发生什么。早一点，比迟到而匆忙更温和。

家庭和同学可以在不竞争的情况下分享他们诚实的用时。知道一张海报通常需要两个晚上，能帮助每个人做计划。测量自己工作的学生，会开始更少与时钟争吵，因为时钟不再是一个意外。这种技能看起来平常，却是后来的学习和工作里最有用的技能之一。要管理时间，你必须先对时间说真话——包括那些你在开始时没有看见的时间。

questions.q: 1. Why do many time plans fail, according to the passage?
options: Only because of laziness
Because the work often takes longer than we guessed, and our sense of time is weak
Because a cook can never know when rice is done
Because a report always fits a thirty-minute box
questions.exp: 文中指出计划失败常因工作比猜测更久，问题是对任务真正用时感觉不足。

questions.q: 2. How can a notebook train a better sense of time?
options: By writing a guess before you start and the real time when you finish, then using the pattern in the next plan
By shaming you whenever writing takes twice as long
By hiding the minutes spent looking for a missing book
By giving every task the same narrow box
questions.exp: 文中建议开始前写下猜测、结束时写下真实时间，用一周的模式给写作更宽的格子。

questions.q: 3. What should a fair estimate include besides the ‘main work’?
options: Nothing but the writing itself
A rule that new tasks must always be guessed as shorter
A fight with the clock at the last moment
The hidden minutes at the edges, such as opening files, walking to the library, or printing, plus a little extra for a hard paragraph
questions.exp: 文中说公平的估计包括打开文件、去图书馆、打印等边缘时间，并为难段留余地。

questions.q: 4. What happens when students measure their work honestly?
options: They must compete with classmates about every minute
They tell less truth about time than before
They start fewer fights with the clock, because the time is no longer a surprise
They can no longer plan a poster that takes two evenings
questions.exp: 文中说测量工作的学生更少与时钟争吵，因为时钟不再是意外。

junior.title: ⬜ Leaving Empty Space in a Busy Calendar
junior.content:
A calendar that is completely full can look like a sign of success. In fact, it is often a trap. When every hour already has a name, a single late bus, a longer lesson, or a friend who needs to talk can break the whole day. Time management is not only the art of adding tasks. It is also the art of leaving empty space, the way a good page leaves margins, so that the important lines can still breathe.

Empty space is not the same as wasted time. It is a reserve. You can use it for a task that ran over, for a short walk when your head is tired, or for the unexpected visit that matters more than a half-finished list. If the space is not used, you can read, practise, or rest, which are also part of a healthy week. Students who fear empty squares sometimes fill them with extra clubs until they are too tired to do any of them well. A smaller number of activities, done with care, often teaches more.

You can protect this space on purpose. After two hard study blocks, keep twenty minutes unnamed. On one weekday evening, refuse a fourth event even if it looks attractive. Tell people, kindly, that you already have a plan for that hour, even if the plan is simply to be free. This is not selfish in a mean way. It is a way of arriving on time, staying kind, and having enough energy for the work you already promised.

Look at your calendar once a week and ask: where could a delay go without ruining the night? If the answer is “nowhere,” the plan is too tight. Move one thing, or shorten one thing, until a margin appears. Busy days will still come, but they will not all crash into one another. Managing time well includes protecting a little quiet, because quiet is where the next good decision has room to be made.
junior.translation:
一份完全被填满的日历，看起来可能像成功的标志。事实上，它常常是一个陷阱。当每一个小时都已经有了名字，一辆晚点的公交车、一节更长的课，或一位需要交谈的朋友，就可能打破整天。时间管理不仅仅是添加任务的艺术。它也是留下空白的艺术，就像一张好的书页会留下页边，好让重要的句子仍然能够呼吸。

空白并不等于浪费的时间。它是一种储备。你可以用它来完成一项超时的任务，在头脑疲倦时短走一会儿，或用来接待一次比一份做了一半的清单更重要的意外来访。如果这段空间没有被用掉，你可以阅读、练习或休息，而这些也是健康的一周的一部分。害怕空白格子的学生，有时会用额外的社团把它们填满，直到累得哪一件都做不好。数量更少、却用心完成的活动，常常教得更多。

你可以有意地保护这片空间。在两段辛苦的学习之后，留二十分钟不要命名。在一个工作日的晚上，即使第四件事看起来吸引人，也拒绝它。善意地告诉别人，那个小时你已经有计划了，即使计划仅仅是让自己空着。这并不是一种刻薄的自私。这是一种准时到达、保持善意、并有足够精力去完成你已经答应的工作的方式。

每周看一次你的日历，并问：一次延误可以去哪里，而不至于毁掉这个晚上？如果答案是“无处可去”，计划就太紧了。移动一件事，或缩短一件事，直到页边出现。忙碌的日子仍然会到来，但它们不会全部撞成一堆。管理时间也包括保护一点点安静，因为下一个好决定，需要在安静里才有空间被做出来。

questions.q: 1. Why can a completely full calendar be a trap?
options: Because empty space is always wasted time
Because margins on a page make important lines harder to read
Because a late bus, a longer lesson, or a friend who needs to talk can then break the whole day
Because success means naming every hour
questions.exp: 文中说每个小时都有名字时，晚点、拖堂或朋友需要交谈就可能打破整天。

questions.q: 2. What is empty space for, if it is not wasted time?
options: Only for extra clubs until you are too tired to do any of them well
A reserve for overtime work, a short walk, an important unexpected visit, or reading and rest if it stays free
A reason to refuse any healthy week
A plan that must never include care or rest
questions.exp: 文中把空白称作储备，可用于超时任务、散步、更重要的来访，或阅读与休息。

questions.q: 3. How can you protect this space on purpose?
options: Keep some minutes unnamed after hard work, and kindly refuse a fourth event if you need to be free
Fill every weekday evening with one more attractive event
Never tell people that an hour is already planned
Use all your energy on tasks you did not promise
questions.exp: 文中建议两段辛苦学习后留二十分钟不命名，并善意拒绝第四件事。

questions.q: 4. What should you do if a delay would have nowhere to go?
options: Leave the plan tight and hope the night is not ruined
Remove all quiet from the week
Stop looking at the calendar
Move or shorten one thing until a margin appears, so busy days do not all crash together
questions.exp: 文中说如果延误无处可去，计划就太紧，应移动或缩短一件事直到页边出现。

junior.title: 🧺 A Weekend Market Where Neighbours Meet
junior.content:
On some weekend mornings, a quiet street becomes a market. Farmers and bakers set out fruit, bread and flowers. A neighbour sells homemade pickles. A student helps a grandparent watch a stall. People come for food, but they also come to meet. They compare the peaches, ask about a child’s school, and loan a bag to someone whose hands are full. A market of this kind is a piece of social life that a supermarket, with all its speed, cannot fully replace. It is a place where the same faces return, and a town feels smaller in a kind way.

The conversations are ordinary and important. A cook shares a way to use a vegetable that is in season. An older person explains which apples store well through the week. A new family asks for directions and is walked to the bus stop. Children learn to wait, to greet, and to count change. These are small lessons in living with others, taught without a classroom. When rain comes, people squeeze under a tent and laugh, and the shared trouble becomes another kind of glue.

Markets also show the work behind daily life. Someone woke early to wash the greens. Someone carried heavy boxes. If we only buy and hurry away, we miss the chance to say thank you, or to notice when a stall needs a hand. Social life grows when buyers and sellers treat one another as neighbours, not only as wallets. A fair price and a clean space are part of that respect. So is returning a borrowed chair at the end of the morning.

Students can be part of this picture: help to set up, make a sign, carry a bag for someone older, or simply say hello instead of looking only at a phone. If your town has no market, a school fair or a small exchange of books and plants can create a similar meeting. Society is not only news on a screen. Sometimes it is a weekend street, a shared table of tomatoes, and the habit of showing up for one another.
junior.translation:
在一些周末的早晨，一条安静的街会变成市场。农人和面包师摆出水果、面包和花。一位邻居出售自制的腌菜。一个学生帮祖父母看着摊位。人们为食物而来，但也是为了相遇而来。他们比较桃子，问起一个孩子的学校，并把袋子借给双手已经拿满的人。这样的市场是社会生活的一部分，再快的超市也不能完全代替。它是同一批面孔会再来的地方，也是一座城镇以一种善意的方式显得更小的地方。

那些对话既平常又重要。一位厨子分享一种当季蔬菜的用法。一位年长的人说明哪些苹果可以存放过这一周。一个新来的家庭问路，并被送到公交站。孩子们学习等待、问候，以及数找回的钱。这些是与他人一起生活的小课，却没有教室。下雨时，人们挤进帐篷里笑着，而这共同的麻烦又变成另一种胶水。

市场也显示日常生活背后的劳动。有人很早起来洗菜。有人扛着沉重的箱子。如果我们只是买了就匆匆离开，就会错过说谢谢的机会，或错过在一个摊位需要帮手时伸出手。当买的人和卖的人把彼此当作邻居，而不仅仅当作钱包时，社会生活就会生长。公平的价格和干净的场地是那种尊重的一部分。早晨结束时归还借来的椅子，也是。

学生可以成为这幅图画的一部分：帮忙摆摊，做一块牌子，为年长的人提袋子，或只是问一声好，而不是只看着手机。如果你的城镇没有市场，一次学校义卖，或一次小小的书本和植物交换，也可以创造相似的相遇。社会不仅仅是屏幕上的新闻。有时它是一条周末的街道，一桌共享的番茄，以及那种为彼此出现的习惯。

questions.q: 1. Why can a weekend market not be fully replaced by a supermarket?
options: Because a supermarket never sells fruit or bread
Because markets refuse to let neighbours talk
Because children are not allowed to count change
Because people come not only for food but also to meet, and the same faces return
questions.exp: 文中说人们为食物而来也为相遇而来，同一批面孔会再来，超市的速度不能完全代替这种社会生活。

questions.q: 2. What small social lessons can children learn at the market?
options: To hurry away without saying thank you
To treat every seller only as a wallet
To wait, to greet, and to count change, and even to share a tent in the rain
To look only at a phone and never say hello
questions.exp: 文中举例等待、问候、数零钱，下雨时挤在帐篷里，都是与他人一起生活的小课。

questions.q: 3. How can buyers and sellers treat one another as neighbours?
options: By ignoring the early work behind the stall
By offering a fair price, a clean space, a thank you, and a returned chair
By never noticing when a stall needs a hand
By refusing any school fair or book exchange
questions.exp: 文中提到说谢谢、帮忙、公平价格、干净场地，以及归还借来的椅子。

questions.q: 4. How can students take part if their town has no market?
options: A school fair or a small exchange of books and plants can create a similar meeting
They cannot meet neighbours in any other way
They should wait for news on a screen and never show up
They must never help to set up or carry a bag
questions.exp: 文中说若没有市场，学校义卖或书本植物交换也可以创造相似的相遇。

junior.title: 🫖 Visiting Older Neighbours Who Live Alone
junior.content:
In many buildings, an older person lives behind a door that rarely opens to guests. They may be independent and proud, and they may also be lonely on a long afternoon. A short visit from a younger neighbour can change the feel of the day: a knock, a bag of fruit, a question about a plant in the hallway, or a shared cup of tea. Social life is not only parties and group chats. It is also these quiet visits that keep a building from becoming a set of locked rooms.

The visit should be respectful. Ask before you come, and accept a “not today” without taking offence. Sit where you are invited to sit. Listen more than you advise. Older neighbours often have stories about the street when it was different, and those stories are part of the area’s living history. You can offer practical help if it is wanted: reaching a high shelf, reading a small print letter, or walking together to the corner shop. The point is company, not a performance of charity that makes the other person feel small.

Families can make this a regular, gentle habit, perhaps once a week, and can include children so that they learn names and manners. A note under the door before a holiday, or a quick hello when you collect the mail, also matters. In very hot or very cold weather, a check-in can be more than polite; it can be important. If you ever worry that someone needs medical help, tell an adult and do not try to handle a serious problem alone.

Students sometimes say they do not know what to talk about. You can begin with something shared: the weather, a festival, a new shop, or a photo in a frame. Silence for a few seconds is allowed. When you leave, say when you might come again, so that the week ahead feels less empty. A neighbourhood is stronger when young and old still know one another by name. That simple knowledge is a kind of social wealth no app can fully store.
junior.translation:
在许多楼里，一位年长的人住在一扇很少对客人打开的门后面。他们也许独立而骄傲，在漫长的下午里也可能孤单。一次来自年轻邻居的短访，可以改变这一天的感觉：一声敲门，一袋水果，一句关于走廊里一盆植物的问候，或共享的一杯茶。社会生活不仅仅是聚会和群聊。它也是这些安静的拜访，好让一栋楼不变成一组锁着的房间。

拜访应当是尊重的。来之前先问过，并接受一句“今天不行”，不要觉得被冒犯。坐在邀请你坐的地方。多听，少给建议。年长的邻居常常有关于这条街从前样子的故事，那些故事是这个区域活着的历史的一部分。如果对方需要，你可以提供实际的帮助：够一个高架子，读一封小字的信，或一起走到转角的店。重点是陪伴，而不是一场让对方觉得自己渺小的慈善表演。

家庭可以把这变成一种规律而温和的习惯，也许一周一次，并可以带上孩子，好让他们学习名字和礼貌。假日前门缝下的一张纸条，或取信件时的一声快速问好，也很重要。在极热或极冷的天气里，一次问候可能不仅是礼貌，它可能很重要。如果你担心有人需要医疗帮助，就告诉成年人，不要独自处理严重的问题。

学生有时会说他们不知道该谈什么。你可以从共同的事物开始：天气，一个节日，一家新店，或相框里的一张照片。几秒钟的安静是被允许的。离开时，说一声你大约何时会再来，好让接下来的一周不那么空。当年轻人和年长的人仍然能叫出彼此的名字时，一个邻里会更强。那种简单的认识，是一种没有应用能完全存储的社会财富。

questions.q: 1. Why can a short visit matter to an older neighbour who lives alone?
options: Because a knock, a conversation or a shared cup of tea can change the feel of a long afternoon
Because social life is only parties and group chats
Because every older person wants a performance of charity
Because locked rooms are the best kind of building
questions.exp: 文中说短访可以改变漫长下午的感觉，使楼不只是一组锁着的房间。

questions.q: 2. What makes a visit respectful?
options: Arriving without asking and giving a lot of advice
Making the other person feel small so that you look kind
Handling a serious medical problem alone
Asking first, accepting a ‘not today’, listening more than advising, and offering help only if it is wanted
questions.exp: 文中强调先询问、接受今天不行、多听少建议，以及在需要时才提供实际帮助。

questions.q: 3. When can a simple check-in be especially important?
options: Only on days when there is no weather at all
When you want to ignore names and manners
In very hot or very cold weather, and you should tell an adult if someone may need medical help
When you plan never to say hello at the mailboxes
questions.exp: 文中指出在极热或极冷天气里，问候可能很重要；若担心需要医疗帮助，应告诉成年人。

questions.q: 4. What should you do if you do not know what to talk about?
options: Leave without a word so the week feels more empty
Begin with something shared, allow a little silence, and say when you might come again
Avoid all photos, festivals and new shops as topics
Refuse to learn the neighbour’s name
questions.exp: 文中建议从天气、节日、新店或照片谈起，允许短暂安静，离开时说明大约何时再来。

junior.title: 🚌 The Unwritten Rules of a Crowded Bus
junior.content:
A crowded bus is a moving room full of strangers who must share a small space for a short time. No teacher stands at the front to recite the rules, yet most people follow a quiet set of customs: queue at the door, let passengers off before you get on, move down the aisle, and offer a seat to someone who needs it more. These unwritten rules are a daily lesson in social life. They show whether a city feels harsh or kind in ordinary minutes, not only in speeches.

The rules work because they reduce friction. If everyone pushed in at once, bags would jam the door and the bus would leave late. If phones were always on loudspeaker, no one could rest or think. A backpack worn on the back in a tight aisle can hit a face; holding it lower is a small act of care. Thanking the driver, or saying “excuse me” instead of a silent shove, keeps the temperature of the trip from rising. None of these acts will appear in a history book, but they shape the mood of a morning.

Visitors and children learn by watching. When a student stands and points to a free seat for a parent with a toddler, other people often copy the kindness. When someone pretends not to see an older passenger, the opposite lesson spreads. Social life is contagious in both directions. Drivers and signs can help, but they cannot replace the hundred small choices made by the people standing in the aisle.

You can practise these customs on your school bus or on a city route. Prepare your card or coin before the stop. Keep your bag out of the way. Offer the seat without making a speech, and accept a “no, thank you” with a smile. If you travel with friends, keep your voices down so that the bus remains a shared space, not a private party. A city is more liveable when strangers can ride together in peace. That peace is built from habits that look tiny until they are missing.
junior.translation:
一辆拥挤的公共汽车，是一间装满陌生人的移动房间，他们必须在短时间里共享一小块空间。没有老师站在前面背诵规则，但大多数人仍然遵守一套安静的习惯：在门口排队，先下后上，往通道里面走，并把座位让给更需要的人。这些不成文的规则，是社会生活里的一堂每日课。它们显示一座城市在平常的几分钟里是刻薄还是善意，而不仅仅在演说里。

这些规则之所以有效，是因为它们减少摩擦。如果所有人一起往里挤，包会堵住门口，车也会晚点离开。如果手机总是外放，就没有人能够休息或思考。在狭窄通道里把背包背在背上，可能会打到一张脸；把它拿低一点，是一个小小的关心。感谢司机，或说一声“借过”而不是沉默地挤，可以不让这一程的温度升高。这些行为都不会出现在历史书里，但它们塑造着一个早晨的心情。

来访的人和孩子通过观看来学习。当一个学生站起来，指着一个空位给带幼儿的家长时，其他人常常会模仿这种善意。当有人假装没看见一位年长的乘客时，相反的课就会传播。社会生活在两个方向上都是会传染的。司机和标牌可以帮忙，但它们不能代替站在通道里的人们所做的那一百个小小选择。

你可以在校车或城市线路上练习这些习惯。在到站前准备好卡或硬币。把包放到不挡路的地方。让座时不必发表演说，并微笑着接受一句“不用，谢谢”。如果和朋友一起出行，把声音放低，好让公共汽车仍然是共享的空间，而不是一场私人聚会。当陌生人能够平静地一起乘坐时，一座城市会更宜居。那份平静，是由一些看起来微小、直到缺失时才被发现的习惯建成的。

questions.q: 1. What unwritten rules of a crowded bus does the passage name first?
options: Push in together so that the bus leaves late
Queue at the door, let people off before you get on, move down the aisle, and offer a seat to someone who needs it more
Keep the phone on loudspeaker at all times
Wear a backpack high so that it can hit a face
questions.exp: 文中首先列举排队、先下后上、往里走，以及把座位让给更需要的人。

questions.q: 2. Why do these rules reduce friction?
options: Because they keep doors from jamming, allow people to rest, and replace a silent shove with a polite word
Because they will all appear in a history book
Because drivers and signs can replace every small choice
Because a private party is the best use of a shared bus
questions.exp: 文中解释一齐挤会堵住门口，外放会使人无法休息，礼貌的“借过”能降低温度。

questions.q: 3. How is social life ‘contagious’ on a bus?
options: Only unkindness can ever spread
Children cannot learn by watching
A student must never point to a free seat
Kindness such as offering a seat is often copied, and so is the habit of pretending not to see someone in need
questions.exp: 文中说让座的善意常被模仿，假装看不见的相反课也会传播，社会生活两个方向都会传染。

questions.q: 4. What should you do when you travel with friends?
options: Leave bags in the aisle and never prepare your card
Make a long speech whenever you offer a seat
Keep your voices down so the bus remains a shared space, not a private party
Refuse a smile if someone says ‘no, thank you’
questions.exp: 文中建议和朋友出行时放低声音，好让车仍是共享空间而不是私人聚会。

junior.title: 👛 Returning a Lost Item Instead of Keeping It
junior.content:
One day you may find a wallet on a bench, a phone on a desk, or a set of keys by the gate. For a second, a small voice may say that no one saw you. Responsibility begins in that second. The honest action is to try to return the item, not to keep it, even if the thing is useful or the owner is unknown. A society works better when lost things have a path home, and when students practise that path while they are young.

There is a safe way to help. Do not post a photo of a bank card or an address on a public wall. Take the item to a teacher, a shop counter, a lost-and-found box, or a parent, and describe where you found it. If a name or a number is visible, an adult can make the call. If you wait beside the object for a few minutes, the owner may come back, which is often the simplest solution. Curiosity about the contents should stop at what is needed to find the person.

Returning something can feel quiet, without a prize. That is part of the lesson. The reward is a neighbourhood where people can drop a bag and still hope. The owner may be anxious, late, or unable to replace a key on the same day. Your action can save them a day of trouble, and it can also protect you from the later discomfort of using what was not yours. If a reward is offered, you may accept or politely refuse; either way, the responsibility has already been met.

Talk about this at home and in class before it happens, so that the choice is already clear. Students can also help by labelling their own things and by checking a lost-and-found shelf when they miss an item. Honesty is not only about tests. It is about the small objects that pass through our hands, and about the kind of community we want to be when no one is filming us. A returned key is a quiet kind of courage.
junior.translation:
有一天，你也许会在长凳上发现一个钱包，在桌上发现一部手机，或在门口发现一串钥匙。有一瞬间，一个小小的声音也许会说：没有人看见你。责任就从那一瞬间开始。诚实的行动是试着把物品还回去，而不是留下它，即使那东西有用，或主人还不知道是谁。当丢失的东西有一条回家的路，当学生在年轻时就练习这条路，一个社会会运转得更好。

帮助有一种安全的方法。不要在公共墙上张贴银行卡或地址的照片。把物品交给老师、商店柜台、失物招领处或家长，并说明你在哪里找到它。如果看得见姓名或号码，可以由成年人来打电话。如果你在物品旁等几分钟，主人也许会回来，而这常常是最简单的办法。对里面东西的好奇，应该止于找到那个人所需要的信息。

归还某件东西，感觉可能很安静，并没有奖品。那也是这一课的一部分。回报是一个人们即使掉了包也仍然可以抱有希望的邻里。主人可能正焦虑、要迟到，或没法在同一天配一把新钥匙。你的行动可以给他们省去一天的麻烦，也可以保护你自己，使你后来不会因为使用了不属于你的东西而不安。如果有人要给报酬，你可以接受，也可以礼貌地拒绝；无论怎样，责任都已经被履行了。

在事情发生之前，就在家里和课堂上谈论这件事，好让选择已经清楚。学生也可以给自己的东西做标记，并在丢失物品时去查看失物招领架。诚实不仅仅与考试有关。它也与从我们手里经过的小物件有关，与当没有人拍摄我们时，我们想成为怎样的共同体有关。一把被送回的钥匙，是一种安静的勇敢。

questions.q: 1. When does responsibility begin after you find a lost item?
options: After you have already decided to keep the useful thing
Only if a camera is filming the bench
In the second when a small voice says that no one saw you, and you choose to try to return it
Only when the owner is already known
questions.exp: 文中说责任从那一声“没有人看见你”的瞬间开始，诚实的行动是试着归还。

questions.q: 2. What is a safe way to help?
options: Post a photo of a bank card or an address on a public wall
Take the item to a teacher, a counter or a lost-and-found, or wait nearby, and let an adult call if a number is visible
Open every part of a wallet out of curiosity
Hide the keys until a prize is promised
questions.exp: 文中建议交给老师、柜台或失物招领，说明地点，由成年人打电话，或在旁等候；不要公开卡和地址。

questions.q: 3. What reward does the passage name even when there is no prize?
options: A neighbourhood where people can still hope after dropping a bag, and the owner may be saved a day of trouble
The later discomfort of using what was not yours
A rule that you must always accept money
A reason not to label your own things
questions.exp: 文中说回报是一个仍可抱有希望的邻里，以及给焦虑的主人省去一天麻烦。

questions.q: 4. How can students prepare before such a moment happens?
options: By refusing to check a lost-and-found shelf
By treating honesty as a matter of tests only
By waiting until someone is filming them before they act
By talking about the choice at home and in class, and by labelling their own things
questions.exp: 文中建议事先在家和课堂上谈论，并给自己的东西做标记，丢失时去查看失物招领。

junior.title: 🧹 Taking Care of a Shared School Space
junior.content:
A school is a shared home for many hours of the week. Hallways, toilets, canteens, labs and playgrounds belong to everyone and to no one person alone. That is why they can become dirty or damaged so quickly, and why taking care of them is a real responsibility, not a job for “somebody else.” A wrapper left on a stair, a wet floor ignored, or a broken hook that no one reports can make the next student’s day harder, and sometimes less safe.

Care looks ordinary. Push in a chair. Wipe a spill if you can do it safely, or tell an adult if you cannot. Return a shared ball, a stapler, or a class set of scissors to the right box. Leave the sink as clean as you hope to find it. These acts take less than a minute, yet they add up. When a whole class treats the room as theirs, the room stays pleasant, and less of the caretaker’s time is spent repairing carelessness. Responsibility is not a speech on a wall. It is a habit that shows up after the bell.

There is also a fairness in this. The people who clean schools work hard, and they should not have to collect easy messes that students could have avoided. Younger children copy older ones. If you walk past litter, you teach a lesson you may not mean to teach. If you pick it up, or if you stop a friend from writing on a desk, you protect a space that does not belong only to you. Reporting damage quickly is part of the same care; hiding it can make the repair more expensive.

Classes can agree on a simple rota for small jobs, and can review it without blame, asking what would make the system easier. Students who practise this at school often take the same eyes into parks and buses. A community is only as strong as its shared rooms. Leaving a place better than you found it, even by a little, is a quiet promise to the people who will walk in after you.
junior.translation:
一所学校在一周的许多小时里，是一个共享的家。走廊、厕所、食堂、实验室和操场属于每一个人，又不属于单独某一个人。这就是为什么它们会那么快变脏或被损坏，以及为什么照料它们是一项真正的责任，而不是“别人”的工作。楼梯上留下的一张包装纸，被忽视的一块湿地板，或没人报告的一个坏钩子，都会让下一个学生的一天更难，有时也更不安全。

照料看起来很平常。把椅子推进去。如果可以安全地擦，就擦掉一摊洒出的水，如果不能，就告诉成年人。把共享的球、订书机，或一套班级剪刀放回正确的盒子。让水槽像你希望找到它时那样干净。这些行动花不了一分钟，却会积累起来。当整一班把房间当作自己的，房间就会保持宜人，勤杂人员的时间也就较少花在修补粗心上。责任不是墙上的一篇演说。它是铃响之后仍会出现的习惯。

这里面也有一种公平。打扫学校的人工作很辛苦，他们不应当再去收拾那些学生本可以避免的、容易的脏乱。更小的孩子会模仿更大的孩子。如果你对垃圾走过去不管，你就在上一堂你也许并不想上的课。如果你捡起来，或阻止朋友在桌上写字，你就是在保护一个并不只属于你的空间。迅速报告损坏也是同样的照料；隐瞒它，可能使修理更加昂贵。

班级可以商定一个简单的轮值来做小工作，并可以在不责备的情况下回顾它，问问怎样能让这个制度更容易。在学校练习这一点的学生，常常会把同样的眼睛带进公园和公共汽车。一个共同体，只有在它的共享房间里一样强。把一个地方留得比你找到时更好，哪怕只好一点点，也是对那些将在你之后走进来的人的一个安静承诺。

questions.q: 1. Why is taking care of school spaces a real responsibility?
options: Because the jobs are only for somebody else
Because a school is never a shared home
Because a broken hook should never be reported
Because hallways and playgrounds belong to everyone, and a wrapper or a wet floor can make the next student’s day harder or less safe
questions.exp: 文中说这些地方属于每个人又不属于单独一人，留下的包装纸或湿地板会让下一个学生更难，有时也不安全。

questions.q: 2. Which ordinary acts of care does the passage mention?
options: Leaving the sink dirty for the caretaker
Writing on a desk so that younger children can copy it
Pushing in a chair, wiping a spill or telling an adult, and returning shared tools to the right box
Hiding damage so that the repair becomes more expensive
questions.exp: 文中列举推椅子、安全地擦洒出的水或告知成人、归还共享用具，以及保持水槽干净。

questions.q: 3. What fairness does the writer point out?
options: Older students should ignore litter so that younger ones can learn to drop it
Cleaners should not have to collect easy messes that students could have avoided
Reporting damage quickly is unnecessary
A rota must always be used to blame someone
questions.exp: 文中指出打扫的人很辛苦，不应再收拾学生本可避免的脏乱。

questions.q: 4. What quiet promise is described at the end?
options: Leaving a place a little better than you found it, for the people who will walk in after you
Taking none of these eyes into parks or buses
Making the shared rooms weaker than the community
Reviewing a rota only in order to assign blame
questions.exp: 文中说把地方留得比找到时更好一点点，是对后来走进来的人的安静承诺。

junior.title: 🔌 Switching Off What We Are Not Using
junior.content:
Lights left on in an empty classroom, a fan running after everyone has left, or a charger glowing on a desk all night may seem like tiny things. Together, they waste electricity that had to be produced, paid for, and often generated in ways that affect the air we share. Switching off what we are not using is a small habit with a public meaning. It is a way students can take responsibility for a cost they do not see on a bill, but that a school and a planet still have to carry.

The habit is practical and easy to teach. The last person out of a room checks the lights and the screen. A class can choose a weekly monitor, not as a police officer, but as a reminder. At home, unplug a charger that has finished its job, and close a door so that heating or cooling does not leak into a hallway. These actions take seconds. Posters help only if the hands follow them. Responsibility grows when the action becomes automatic, like fastening a seat belt, rather than a once-a-year slogan.

There is a fair question: does one switch matter? One switch, once, is small. Many switches, every day, in every classroom, are not. Schools that measure their use often find that empty rooms were quietly expensive. The lesson is not to sit in the dark or to fear every machine. It is to match the energy to the need, and to notice when the need has ended. Science class can explain where the power comes from; the hallway is where the idea becomes a choice.

Students can also speak up kindly: “Shall I turn this off?” is enough. If a machine must stay on for a reason, learn that reason instead of guessing. Share the habit with younger children so that it feels normal, not nagging. A responsible community does not wait for a perfect law before it starts to care. It begins with the nearest switch, and with the understanding that shared resources are part of our shared future.
junior.translation:
空教室里还亮着的灯，所有人离开后仍在转的风扇，或整晚在桌上发着光的充电器，看起来都可能像小事。它们合在一起，却会浪费必须被生产、被付费，并且常常以影响我们共享的空气的方式被制造出来的电。关掉我们并不在使用的东西，是一个具有公共意义的小习惯。这是学生可以为一种他们在账单上看不见、但学校和地球仍然必须承担的成本负起责任的方式。

这个习惯很实际，也容易教。最后一个离开房间的人检查灯和屏幕。一个班级可以选出每周的巡视员，不是作为警察，而是作为提醒。在家里，拔掉已经完成工作的充电器，并关上门，好让供暖或制冷不漏进走廊。这些行动只需几秒。只有手跟上去，海报才有用。当行动变得像系安全带一样自动，而不是一年一次的口号时，责任就会生长。

有一个公平的问题：按一下开关有关系吗？一次、一下，是小的。每一天、每一间教室里的许多开关，就不是小的。测量过用电的学校，常常发现空房间一直在悄悄地昂贵着。这一课不是让人坐在黑暗里，或害怕每一台机器。它是让能量匹配需要，并在需要结束时注意到它。科学课可以解释电从哪里来；走廊，则是这个想法变成一种选择的地方。

学生也可以善意地开口：“我把它关掉好吗？”就足够了。如果一台机器必须因某个原因保持开着，就去了解那个原因，而不是猜测。和更小的孩子分享这个习惯，好让它感觉是正常的，而不是唠叨。一个负责任的共同体，不会等一部完美的法律到来才开始关心。它从最近的那个开关开始，也从一种理解开始：共享的资源，是我们共同未来的一部分。

questions.q: 1. Why is switching off unused lights and chargers a public kind of responsibility?
options: Because the wasted electricity must still be produced, paid for, and often generated in ways that affect the air we share
Because a glowing charger at night has no cost at all
Because students can already see every school bill
Because empty classrooms never use power
questions.exp: 文中指出浪费的电仍须被生产、付费，并常常以影响共享空气的方式产生。

questions.q: 2. Which practical habits does the passage recommend?
options: Leaving doors open so that heating leaks into the hallway
Putting up posters and never using hands
Acting only during a once-a-year slogan
The last person out checks lights and the screen, a weekly reminder is chosen, and finished chargers are unplugged
questions.exp: 文中建议最后离开的人检查灯和屏幕，设每周提醒，用完的充电器要拔掉，并关门以免冷暖泄漏。

questions.q: 3. How does the writer answer the question ‘does one switch matter?’
options: One switch never matters, so we should sit in the dark always
Schools that measure use never find any waste
One switch once is small, but many switches every day in every classroom are not, and empty rooms can be quietly expensive
Every machine should be feared and left on
questions.exp: 文中说按一下一次是小的，但每天每间教室的许多开关就不是，空房间可能悄悄地昂贵。

questions.q: 4. What kind sentence can students use to speak up?
options: A nagging speech that never includes younger children
‘Shall I turn this off?’, and they should learn the reason if a machine must stay on
A demand for a perfect law before any care begins
A guess that every machine must stay on forever

junior.title: 🍽️ Putting the Phone Away When We Eat Together
junior.content:
A phone can be useful at the table: it can show a recipe, pay a bill, or catch a quick message from a family member who is late. It can also steal the meal. When every person looks down at a bright screen, the shared table becomes a set of private islands. Putting the phone away for the length of dinner is a small modern habit that protects an old kind of life: talking, tasting, and noticing the people in the same room.

The habit works better with a clear place. A basket in the middle of the table, a shelf by the door, or a silent mode in another room can hold the devices until the plates are empty. Families can agree on exceptions: a call from a grandparent, a timer for the oven, or an emergency. The point is not to hate technology. The point is to decide when it is a guest at the meal and when it is an interruption. Children copy what they see. If adults scroll through the whole soup, a rule for children only will feel unfair.

There are practical gains as well. Food tastes more distinct when your eyes are on the plate, not on a video. Conversation has room to grow past one-word answers. People chew more slowly, which is kinder to the body. A meal without a screen is also a rest for tired eyes after a day of study or work. Guests feel more welcome when they do not have to compete with a glowing rectangle for your face.

Students can practise this at lunch, too, by keeping the phone in a bag unless they truly need it, and by choosing talk with a classmate over a short video. If a message is urgent, they can step aside, answer, and return. Technology is part of daily life, and it will stay. The skill is to give it a time and a place, so that a simple meal can still be a meeting, not a set of separate screens around a table.
junior.translation:
一部手机在餐桌上可以有用：它能显示一份食谱，支付账单，或接收一位迟到的家人的短讯。它也可以偷走这顿饭。当每个人都低头看着一块发亮的屏幕时，共享的桌子就变成一组私人的岛。在用餐的时间里把手机放在一边，是一个保护一种古老生活的小小现代习惯：交谈，品尝，并注意到同一间房间里的人。

这个习惯在有一个明确位置时会更好用。桌子中间的一个篮子，门边的一个架子，或另一间房里的静音模式，都可以在盘子空之前保管这些设备。家庭可以商定例外：祖父母的来电，烤箱的计时器，或紧急情况。重点不是憎恨科技。重点是决定它何时是餐桌上的客人，何时是一种打断。孩子会模仿他们所看见的。如果成年人在整碗汤的时间里都在滑动屏幕，一条只针对孩子的规则就会显得不公平。

这也有实际的益处。当眼睛在盘子上而不是在视频上时，食物的味道会更分明。对话有空间从单字的回答里生长出来。人们会嚼得更慢，这对身体更温和。一顿没有屏幕的饭，也是在一天的学习或工作之后，给疲倦的眼睛一次休息。当客人不必和一块发光的长方形竞争你的脸时，他们会感觉更受欢迎。

学生也可以在午餐时练习这一点：除非真正需要，否则把手机放在包里，并选择和同学交谈，而不是看一条短视频。如果一条消息很紧急，他们可以走到一边，回答，再回来。科技是日常生活的一部分，它也会留下来。技能在于给它一个时间和一个地点，好让一顿简单的饭仍然可以是一次相遇，而不是一圈围着桌子的、彼此分开的屏幕。

questions.q: 1. What old kind of life can putting the phone away during dinner protect?
options: A set of private islands around the table
Talking, tasting, and noticing the people in the same room
A rule that technology must never pay a bill or show a recipe
A habit of scrolling through the whole soup
questions.exp: 文中说把手机放在一边是为了保护交谈、品尝并注意到同一房间里的人。
