senior.title: 🗺️ How a Navigation App Changes the City You Think You Know
senior.content:
A phone that speaks the next turn has made getting lost rarer, and it has changed more than the journey time. People who once built a mental map — a river on the left, a school on the corner, the feeling of a district — can now travel across a city as a series of blue lines and estimated minutes. The convenience is real: a visitor finds a hospital; a night bus is not missed; a driver avoids a closed bridge. Technology and daily life meet here in a trade that is easy to ignore. What we gain in efficiency, we may lose in a kind of local knowledge that used to come free with the walk.

The app does not only show a path. It ranks paths. Its suggestions can send a stream of cars down a once-quiet residential street, or lead pedestrians through a passage that is legal but unfriendly after dark. Shopkeepers on a former main route may see fewer passers-by when the algorithm prefers a faster bypass. The map is a model, updated from other users’ traces, and models have blind spots: a new fence, a flooded underpass, a neighbourhood that is not well photographed. Users who follow the voice without looking up may walk into these gaps. They may also never discover the bakery that is thirty metres off the recommended line, or the park that would have made the same trip kinder.

There is a civic layer to this quiet change. When many people outsource wayfinding, public signs, paper maps and the habit of asking a stranger can wither. A city becomes slightly less knowable to the person whose battery dies. Emergency workers still need streets that humans can describe, not only pins. Children who are driven or navigated everywhere may grow up with weaker spatial confidence, which is a skill, not a luxury. None of this is an argument for throwing the phone away. It is an argument for sometimes using it as a backup, and for looking at the city with the eyes as well as the earpiece.

A healthier habit is mixed. Use the app to enter an unfamiliar area, then try the return on memory, or put the phone in a pocket for one familiar commute a week and notice what you had stopped seeing. Check a second source if a route looks odd. Be cautious about a shortcut through a place you would not walk with a friend. If you drive, remember that a faster line on a screen can still be a harm on a street where children play.

Students can draw, once, a freehand map of their route to school, then compare it with the app’s version: what did they know that the line omitted, and what did the line reveal? Technology that orients us is a gift. Technology that replaces all orientation is a thinner daily life. A city is more than a corridor between pins. It is a set of places that can still be learned, if we occasionally look up from the next instruction and let ourselves, a little, risk being briefly unsure.
senior.translation:
一部会说出下一个转弯的手机会使迷路变得更少，而它改变的也不只是旅程时间。那些曾经建立过心理地图的人——左边一条河，转角一所学校，一个区域的感觉——现在可以把穿越一座城市，变成一串蓝线和估计的分钟。便利是真实的：一位访客找到医院；一班夜车没有错过；一位司机避开一座关闭的桥。科技与日常生活在这里的交换，很容易被忽略。我们在效率上得到的，也许会在一种曾经随着步行免费到来的地方知识上失去。

应用显示的不只是一条路。它给路径排序。它的建议可以把一串汽车送进一条曾经安静的居住街，或把行人领进一段合法、却在天黑后不友好的通道。当算法更喜欢一条更快的旁路时，从前主路上的店主也许会看见更少的路人。这张地图是一个模型，用其他用户的痕迹更新，而模型有盲点：一道新的栅栏，一条被水淹的地下通道，一个没有被好好拍照的街区。不抬头、只跟着声音走的用户，也许会走进这些缺口。他们也许也永远发现不了推荐线路三十米之外的那家面包店，或那座本可以让同一趟旅程更善意的公园。

这种安静的改变有一个公民的层面。当许多人把寻路外包出去时，公共路牌、纸质地图以及向陌生人问路的习惯就可能萎缩。一座城市对电池耗尽的人会稍稍变得更不可知。应急人员仍然需要人类能够描述的街道，而不仅仅是图钉。那些到处都被开车送达或被导航的孩子，也许会在空间自信上较弱地长大，而这是一种技能，不是奢侈。这都不是把手机扔掉的论据。这是一种论据：有时把它当作备份来使用，并用眼睛和耳机一起看这座城市。

一种更健康的习惯是混合的。用应用进入一个不熟悉的区域，然后凭记忆尝试返回，或在一周里把手机放进口袋完成一次熟悉的通勤，并注意你已经停止看见的东西。如果一条路线看起来奇怪，就核对第二个来源。对一条你不会和朋友一起走的近路保持小心。如果你开车，记住屏幕上一条更快的线，仍然可能在孩子们玩耍的街上成为一种伤害。

学生可以有一次徒手画出他们去学校的路，然后把它与应用的版本比较：他们知道哪些被那条线省略了的东西，以及那条线揭示了什么？为我们定向的技术是一份礼物。替换掉所有定向的技术，则是一种更薄的日常生活。一座城市不仅仅是图钉之间的走廊。它是一组仍然可以被学习的地方，如果我们偶尔从下一条指令上抬起头来，并允许自己稍微冒一点短暂不确定的险。

questions.q: 1. What trade does the passage say is easy to ignore when a navigation app saves time?
options: What we gain in efficiency, we may lose in local knowledge that used to come free with the walk, as a city becomes a series of blue lines
Getting lost has become more common, and hospitals are harder to find
A mental map is always stronger when it is only estimated minutes
A closed bridge can never be avoided with an app
questions.exp: 文中说我们在效率上得到的，可能在曾经随步行免费到来的地方知识上失去。

questions.q: 2. How can an app’s ranking of paths affect streets and shops?
options: The map has no blind spots, because it is updated from users’ traces
A legal passage is always friendly after dark
A bakery thirty metres off the line is always discovered by users who never look up
It can send cars down a quiet residential street, lead pedestrians through an unfriendly passage, or take passers-by away from a former main route
questions.exp: 文中举例把车流引入安静居住街、把行人领进天黑后不友好的通道，或使旧主路店主失去路人。

questions.q: 3. What civic layer appears when many people outsource wayfinding?
options: Emergency workers need only pins, never streets humans can describe
The passage argues that everyone should throw the phone away
Public signs, paper maps and asking a stranger may wither, a dead battery leaves a person less able to know the city, and children may grow up with weaker spatial confidence
Spatial confidence is a luxury, not a skill
questions.exp: 文中指出公共路牌与问路习惯可能萎缩，电池耗尽时城市更不可知，孩子的空间自信可能变弱。

questions.q: 4. What mixed habit does the writer recommend?
options: Follow every faster line on a screen, even on a street where children play
Use the app to enter an unfamiliar area, try the return on memory, put the phone away on one familiar commute, check an odd route, and be cautious about unfriendly shortcuts
Never use the app as a backup in an unfamiliar area
Look only with the earpiece, never with the eyes
questions.exp: 文中建议用应用进入陌生区域，凭记忆返回，熟悉通勤偶尔不用手机，并小心不友好的近路。

questions.q: 5. What can a freehand map of the route to school reveal?
options: What the student knew that the app’s line omitted, and what the line revealed, reminding us that a city is more than a corridor between pins
That technology which orients us should replace all orientation
That we should never look up from the next instruction
That being briefly unsure is never a useful risk
questions.exp: 文中建议徒手画去学校的路并与应用比较，看哪些被省略、哪些被揭示，城市不只是图钉之间的走廊。

senior.title: 💳 When Paying Without Cash Becomes the Default, Who Is Left Out?
senior.content:
In many cities it is now possible to buy a ticket, a meal, or a bag of fruit without touching a coin. A card, a phone, or a code at the till is fast, tracks spending, and reduces the cash a shop must guard. For a traveller or a student in a hurry, the convenience is obvious. Technology and daily life have, in this quiet shift, rewritten an ancient habit: the exchange of a physical token. The ethical question is what happens to the people and the situations that the new default does not fit — the elderly person who does not trust a phone, the child without a card, the stall with a weak signal, the customer whose payment is declined for a reason they cannot see, the worker who prefers cash because a digital record feels like surveillance.

A cashless default can widen a kind of everyday inequality. Banks, identification, a stable phone battery, and a signal become tickets of entry to ordinary life. When a café or a bus accepts only electronic payment, those tickets are no longer optional. Fees may be hidden in the price, or in a charge that a poorer customer feels more sharply. Outages and cyberattacks, even if rare, can freeze a street that no longer has a paper backup. Privacy changes too: a cash purchase leaves a thinner trail than a card that tells a company when and where you eat. Some people are happy to trade that trail for points and ease. Others are not, and they should not have to leave the market in order to keep a little opacity.

None of this is an argument that cash is always safer or fairer. Cash can be lost, stolen, or used in hidden labour that harms workers. Digital payment can protect a person from carrying a large sum, can help a small business count honestly, and can make a family budget visible. The better path is usually mixed and deliberate: keep more than one way to pay, especially for essential services; make the fee and the data use clear; provide a human path when a machine says no; and do not treat a lack of a smartphone as a personal failure.

Cities and companies make the climate. A transport system that remains usable with cash or a simple card includes more residents than one that requires a high-end phone. A market that keeps at least some stalls cash-friendly protects a different crowd than a food court of scanners only. Regulation can limit hidden fees and can require a backup during outages. Customers can ask, politely, whether cash is still possible, so that the option does not die of silence.

Students can notice, for a week, where they could not have paid if their battery had died, and who in their family would have been stuck. Technology that speeds a queue is a genuine gift. Technology that becomes the only door to a loaf of bread is a different political fact. A fair daily life leaves more than one way to complete an ordinary purchase, so that innovation does not quietly evict the people who moved more slowly into the new tool.
senior.translation:
在许多城市里，现在可以不碰一枚硬币就买到一张票、一顿饭，或一袋水果。一张卡、一部手机，或柜台处的一个码，很快，能追踪开支，并减少商店必须看守的现金。对一位匆忙的旅行者或学生来说，便利是明显的。科技与日常生活在这场安静的转变里，改写了一种古老的习惯：交换一种物理的代币。伦理问题是，那些新的默认并不适合的人和情境会发生什么——不信任手机的老人，没有卡的孩子，信号很弱的摊位，付款因一个他们看不见的理由被拒绝的顾客，以及因为数字记录感觉像监视而更喜欢现金的工作者。

一种无现金的默认，可以扩大一种日常的不平等。银行、身份证明、稳定的手机电量和信号，都变成进入普通生活的门票。当一家咖啡馆或一辆公共汽车只接受电子支付时，那些门票就不再是可选的。费用也许被藏在价格里，或藏在一种更穷的顾客感觉更尖锐的收费里。故障和网络攻击即使少见，也可以冻结一条不再有纸质备份的街道。隐私也会改变：一次现金购买留下的痕迹，比一张告诉公司你何时何地吃饭的卡更薄。有些人乐于用那条痕迹交换积分和轻松。另一些人不愿意，而他们不应当为了保留一点不透明，就不得不离开市场。

这都不是说现金总是更安全或更公平。现金可以丢失、被偷，或被用于伤害工人的隐蔽劳动。数字支付可以保护一个人不必携带大笔现金，可以帮助小生意诚实计数，也可以使一份家庭预算变得可见。更好的道路通常是混合而有意的：尤其是对基本服务，保持不止一种付款方式；把费用和数据用途说清楚；当机器说不时提供一条人际的路；并且不要把缺少智能手机当作一种个人失败。

城市和公司制造这种气候。一套仍然可以用现金或一张简单的卡来使用的交通系统，比一套需要高端手机的系统，包括更多居民。一个至少让一些摊位对现金友好的市场，保护的人群也不同于一个全是扫描器的美食广场。监管可以限制隐藏费用，并可以要求在故障期间有备份。顾客可以礼貌地询问现金是否仍然可能，好让这个选项不因沉默而死去。

学生可以用一周注意，如果电池耗尽他们在哪里就无法付款，以及家里谁会被卡住。加快队列的技术是一份真正的礼物。变成买一块面包的唯一扇门的技术，则是一种不同的政治事实。一种公平的日常生活，会留下不止一种完成一次平常购买的方式，好让创新不会悄悄地驱逐那些更慢走进新工具的人。

questions.q: 1. What ethical question does a cashless default raise?
options: Whether a card or a code can never be convenient for a traveller
What happens to people and situations the new default does not fit, such as an elderly person without a trusted phone, a stall with a weak signal, or a worker who fears digital surveillance
Whether the exchange of a physical token was never an ancient habit
Whether shops must always guard more cash than before
questions.exp: 文中问新默认不适合的人会怎样，并举例不信任手机的老人、弱信号摊位，以及担心监视的工作者。

questions.q: 2. How can a cashless-only café or bus widen everyday inequality?
options: Banks, identification, a charged phone and a signal become required tickets of entry, fees may hit poorer customers harder, and outages can freeze a street with no paper backup
Privacy always improves, because a card leaves a thinner trail than cash
A poorer customer never feels a hidden fee more sharply
Everyone is happy to trade a spending trail for points and ease
questions.exp: 文中指出银行、证件、电量和信号变成入场券，费用可能对穷人更尖锐，故障可使没有纸质备份的街道停摆。

questions.q: 3. Why is the better path usually mixed and deliberate?
options: Cash is always safer and fairer than any digital record
A lack of a smartphone should be treated as a personal failure
Essential services should accept only one high-end phone method

Cash can be lost or used in hidden labour, and digital payment can be safer and clearer, so essential services should keep more than one way to pay, with clear fees and a human path when a machine says no
questions.exp: 文中说现金与数字各有风险与益处，更好的是混合：基本服务保留多种方式，费用清楚，机器拒绝时有人际路径。

questions.q: 4. How can cities, companies and customers keep the option alive?
options: A food court of scanners only, with no regulation
Letting the cash option die of silence, without polite questions
Transport usable with cash or a simple card, some cash-friendly stalls, limits on hidden fees, backups during outages, and customers who still ask whether cash is possible
Requiring a high-end phone for every bus ride
questions.exp: 文中建议交通系统接受现金或简单卡，市场保留部分现金摊位，监管限制隐藏费用，顾客仍询问现金是否可用。

questions.q: 5. What should students notice in a one-week observation?
options: That a faster queue is always a political problem
Where they could not have paid if their battery had died, and who in their family would have been stuck, because a fair daily life leaves more than one way to buy a loaf of bread
That innovation should quietly evict people who moved slowly into the new tool
That a single door to a loaf of bread is always a genuine gift
questions.exp: 文中建议用一周观察电池耗尽时何处无法付款、家里谁会卡住，公平的日常应保留不止一种购买方式。

senior.title: ↔️ Lateral Reading: Checking the Source Before You Trust the Page
senior.content:
A common way to judge a webpage is to stay on it: read the About section, look for a professional design, and count the footnotes. Professional fact-checkers often do the opposite. They leave the page almost at once and open new tabs to ask who is behind it, what other reliable sources say about this organisation, and whether the claim already has a track record. This habit is called lateral reading. It is a core skill of information literacy in an age when a site can look careful and still be a campaign, a shop, or a hoax. The first page is a performance. The surrounding web is where the performance can be checked.

The method is simple and slightly rude to the page in front of you. Search the organisation’s name plus a word such as “funding,” “review,” or “fact check.” See whether a library, a major newspaper, a scientific body, or a respected watchdog describes it in a way that matches its self-portrait. If the only praise comes from copies of the same text, be cautious. If experts in the field ignore the site, or if they document a pattern of errors, the beautiful layout should not save it. Wikipedia, used carefully as a starting map rather than as a final authority, can show disputes and further links. The aim is not to outsource all judgement. It is to place the document in a landscape before you invest an hour in its argument.

Lateral reading also helps when a post is a screenshot, a video, or a quote with no link. Search a distinctive sentence; look for the original context; see whether the date, the place, or the ending was cropped. A claim that cannot be found outside a closed group, or that appears only on sites that all cite one another, has not yet earned trust. Speed matters because outrage is designed to keep you on the first surface. The thirty seconds spent leaving the page are often the most valuable seconds in the encounter.

Students can practise with two open windows on a controversial claim: one for the original, one for a search about the author and the organisation. Write one sentence on who benefits if you believe it, and one on what a more established source says. Teachers can reward the search path, not only the final opinion. Information literacy is not a personality trait called scepticism. It is a set of moves that can be taught, timed, and improved.

A reader who only travels vertically, deeper into a single site, can be led a long way by a confident voice. A reader who travels sideways, into other rooms of the web, is harder to capture. The web is not only a library. It is also a stage. Lateral reading is how you check the programme before you settle into the seat.
senior.translation:
判断一个网页的常见方式，是留在它上面：读“关于我们”，看专业的设计，并数脚注。专业的事实核查者常常做相反的事。他们几乎立刻离开这个页面，打开新的标签页，去问它背后是谁，其他可靠来源如何谈论这个组织，以及这个主张是否已经有一份记录。这种习惯叫做横向阅读。它是信息素养在这样一个时代里的核心技能：一个站点可以看起来很仔细，却仍然是一场运动、一家商店，或一个骗局。第一页是一场表演。周围的网络，才是表演可以被检查的地方。

这种方法很简单，对眼前的页面也略微有一点不客气。搜索这个组织的名字，加上“资金”“评论”或“事实核查”这样的词。看一座图书馆、一家主要报纸、一个科学机构，或一个受尊重的监督者对它的描述，是否与它的自画像相符。如果唯一的赞美来自同一段文字的复制，就要小心。如果这个领域的专家忽略这个站点，或他们记录了一连串错误，漂亮的版面就不应当救它。谨慎地作为起始地图、而不是最终权威来使用的维基百科，可以显示争论和进一步的链接。目的不是把所有判断外包出去。而是在你把一小时投资进它的论证之前，先把这份文件放进一片风景里。

当帖子是一张截图、一段视频，或一句没有链接的引语时，横向阅读也有帮助。搜索一句有特色的句子；寻找最初的语境；看日期、地点或结尾是否被裁掉。一个在封闭群体之外找不到、或只出现在彼此引用的站点上的主张，还没有赢得信任。速度很重要，因为愤怒被设计来把你留在第一层表面。花在离开这个页面上的三十秒，常常是这次遭遇里最有价值的秒。

学生可以在一个有争议的主张上用两扇打开的窗口练习：一扇给原文，一扇给关于作者和组织的搜索。写下一句如果相信它谁会受益，以及一句更成名的来源怎么说。老师可以奖励这条搜索路径，而不仅仅是最终意见。信息素养不是一种叫做怀疑的性格特质。它是一套可以被教、被计时、被改进的动作。

一个只垂直旅行、向单个站点更深处走的读者，可以被一个自信的声音带得很远。一个向旁边走、走进网络其他房间的读者，更难被俘获。网络不仅仅是一座图书馆。它也是一座舞台。横向阅读，就是你在坐进座位之前先检查节目单的方式。

questions.q: 1. How does lateral reading differ from staying on a page and judging its design and footnotes?
options: It means reading the About section more slowly and counting more footnotes
A professional design is already enough to prove a site is not a campaign or a hoax
Fact-checkers leave the page to ask who is behind it, what reliable sources say about the organisation, and whether the claim has a track record
The first page is never a performance, so the surrounding web need not be checked
questions.exp: 文中说横向阅读是立刻离开页面，查询组织背景、可靠来源的评价以及主张的记录。

questions.q: 2. What should you look for when you search an organisation’s name plus ‘funding’ or ‘fact check’?
options: Whether a beautiful layout can save a site that experts document as error-prone
Whether a library, newspaper, scientific body or watchdog describes it in a way that matches its self-portrait, and whether praise is only copied text
Whether Wikipedia must be used as a final authority, never as a starting map
Whether you should invest an hour before placing the document in a landscape
questions.exp: 文中建议看权威机构的描述是否与自画像相符，并警惕同一段赞美被反复复制。

questions.q: 3. How can lateral reading help with a screenshot or a quote that has no link?
options: Search a distinctive sentence, find the original context, and see whether the date, place or ending was cropped
Trust a claim that appears only on sites that all cite one another
Stay on the first surface, because outrage is a reliable guide
Assume a closed group is a sufficient source if the quote feels sharp
questions.exp: 文中建议搜索特色句子、找回语境，并检查日期地点或结尾是否被裁切。

questions.q: 4. What two-window practice is suggested for students?
options: Reward only the final opinion, never the search path
Treat information literacy as a personality trait that cannot be taught
Close the search window, and travel only deeper into a single site
One window for the original, one for a search about the author, plus a sentence on who benefits and what a more established source says
questions.exp: 文中建议一窗看原文、一窗查作者与组织，并写下谁受益以及更成名来源怎么说。

questions.q: 5. Why is a sideways reader harder to capture than a vertical one?
options: The web is only a library, never a stage
Settling into the first page is the best check of a performance
Leaving the first site for other rooms of the web checks the programme before you settle into the seat, whereas a confident voice can lead a vertical reader a long way
Sideways travel makes judgement impossible
questions.exp: 文中把网络比作舞台：横向走进其他房间是先检查节目单，只向单页纵深则易被自信的声音带走。

senior.title: 📊 How a Chart Can Mislead Even When the Numbers Are Real
senior.content:
A graph looks like neutrality. Axes, bars and a clean title can make a claim feel more scientific than the same claim in words. Information literacy has to include a second look at pictures of numbers, because many misleading charts do not invent data. They choose a window, a scale, or a comparison that pushes the eye toward a conclusion the numbers do not fully earn. A vertical axis that does not start at zero can make a small change look like a crisis. Two charts with different time spans can make the same economy look like a boom or a collapse. A colourful map can shout a difference that, in the table, is tiny.

The first questions are almost rude, and they are necessary. What exactly is being counted, and over what period? Is the baseline fair, or was a high or low year chosen to dramatise a trend? Are the groups comparable, or is a rate being placed beside a raw count? Has a correlation been drawn as if it were a cause? Is there a missing uncertainty, a tiny sample, or a second series that would change the story if it were plotted? A legend that is hard to read, a 3-D bar that distorts height, or a pie chart with too many slices can do the same work as a loud adjective. The design is part of the argument, even when the designer claims to be only “showing the data.”

Good practice runs the other way. Start the axis at a value that does not hide the scale of the change; or, if a zoom is needed, say so clearly. Show the time window you did not choose, if it is relevant. Prefer rates when populations differ. Separate a visual that explores a question from a visual that is built to persuade in a campaign. Journalists and scientists who care about trust often publish the table as well as the picture, and they tell you the source. Readers who care can try to redraw the claim in a simpler form: a sentence with the units, the dates, and the size of the difference.

Students can collect one chart from a news site or a social post each week and write three lines: what it shows, what it suggests, and what it hides. Swap with a classmate and see whether they find a different hiding place. In mathematics or civics, they can be asked to make two honest and two pushy versions of the same small data set, which is a memorable way to feel how much power sits in the axis. Information literacy is not hostility to every graphic. It is the refusal to let a picture do your thinking without a warrant.

A number can be true and still be dressed to mislead. The skilled reader thanks the chart for making a pattern visible, then asks whether another honest picture of the same facts would still support the headline. If the answer is no, the problem was never the arithmetic. It was the costume.
senior.translation:
一张图看起来像中立。轴、柱和一个干净的标题，可以使一个主张感觉比用词语说出的同一个主张更科学。信息素养必须包括对数字图画的第二眼，因为许多误导的图表并不编造数据。它们选择一个窗口、一个尺度，或一种比较，把眼睛推向这些数字并未完全赢得的结论。一条并非从零开始的纵轴，可以使一次小的变化看起来像一场危机。两张时间跨度不同的图，可以使同一种经济看起来像繁荣或崩溃。一张彩色的地图，可以喊出在表里其实很小的差异。

最先的问题几乎有一点不客气，而它们是必要的。被计算的究竟是什么，以及在什么时期里？基线公平吗，还是选了一个高或低的年份来戏剧化一种趋势？这些组可以比较吗，还是把一个比率放在了一个原始计数旁边？一种相关是否被画得仿佛它就是原因？是否缺少不确定性、样本很小，或有第二条如果被画上就会改变故事的系列？一个难读的图例，一根扭曲高度的立体柱，或一张切片太多的饼图，可以做和一个大声形容词同样的工作。设计是论证的一部分，即使设计者声称只是在“展示数据。”

好的做法朝另一个方向走。把轴开始在一个不会隐藏变化尺度的值上；或者，如果需要放大，就清楚地说出来。如果相关，就展示你没有选择的时间窗口。当人口不同时，更喜欢使用比率。把一张探索问题的图，与一张为运动去说服而建的图分开。在乎信任的记者和科学家，常常既发表表也发表图，并告诉你来源。在乎的读者可以试着用更简单的形式重画这个主张：一句带有单位、日期和差异大小的话。

学生可以每周从新闻网站或社交帖子里收集一张图，并写三行：它显示了什么，它暗示了什么，以及它隐藏了什么。和同学交换，看他们是否找到不同的隐藏处。在数学或公民课上，可以要求他们用同一小组数据做出两个诚实的版本和两个带推力的版本，这是感觉轴里坐着多少力量的一种难忘方式。信息素养不是对每一张图的敌意。它是拒绝让一张没有令状的图画代替你思考。

一个数字可以是真的，却仍然被打扮来误导。熟练的读者感谢这张图使一种模式可见，然后问：同一组事实的另一张诚实的图画，是否仍然支持这个标题。如果答案是否定的，问题从来不是算术。而是那套服装。

questions.q: 1. How can a chart mislead even when the numbers are real?
options: By always inventing the data behind the bars
By making every small change look tiny, never like a crisis
By refusing to use colour, titles or maps
By choosing a window, a scale or a comparison that pushes the eye toward a conclusion the numbers do not fully earn, such as an axis that does not start at zero
questions.exp: 文中说明误导图表往往不编造数据，而是通过窗口、尺度或比较推动眼睛，例如纵轴不从零开始。

questions.q: 2. Which questions should you ask of a graph first?
options: Whether a 3-D bar or a busy pie chart can never distort the argument
Whether the designer who claims to be ‘showing the data’ has left design out of the argument
What is counted and over what period, whether the baseline is fair, whether groups are comparable, whether a correlation is drawn as a cause, and whether uncertainty or a second series is missing
Whether a rate may always sit beside a raw count without a problem
questions.exp: 文中列出计数对象与时期、基线是否公平、组是否可比较、相关是否被当成因果，以及是否缺少不确定性或另一条系列。

questions.q: 3. What does good practice do instead?
options: Hide the scale of the change, and never say when a zoom is used
Use a fair axis or label a zoom, show a relevant unused time window, prefer rates when populations differ, and publish the table, the source, and a plain sentence with units and dates
Mix a campaign visual with an exploratory one without a distinction
Leave units, dates and the size of the difference out of any sentence
questions.exp: 文中建议公正的轴或标明放大、展示相关的其他时间窗口、人口不同时用比率，并同时公布表与来源。

questions.q: 4. What weekly exercise can students do with a news or social chart?
options: Write what it shows, what it suggests, and what it hides, then swap with a classmate; or make honest and pushy versions of the same small data set
Treat information literacy as hostility to every graphic
Let the picture do the thinking without a warrant
Avoid asking whether another honest picture would still support the headline
questions.exp: 文中建议每周写三行：显示、暗示与隐藏，并可用同一数据做出诚实与带推力的两个版本。

questions.q: 5. If another honest picture of the same facts would not support the headline, where was the problem?
options: In the refusal to thank a chart for making a pattern visible
In the fact that a number can never be true
In the reader’s wish to count units and dates
Not in the arithmetic, but in the costume — a true number dressed to mislead
questions.exp: 文中说若另一张诚实的图不再支持标题，问题不在算术而在那套“服装”。

senior.title: 🛤️ Why a Road, a Rail, or a Canal Keeps Teaching After the Builders Are Gone
senior.content:
A speech lasts a day; a road can last a century. One of the quiet lessons of history is that infrastructure — rails, ports, canals, power lines, housing estates, school maps — continues to shape lives long after the ceremony at which it was opened. A railway that favoured one port can make another city shrink. A highway cut through a neighbourhood can divide it for generations. A dam can bring light and also drown a valley’s memory. When we ask what the past still has to teach, it is tempting to look only at wars, laws and great books. The built world is also a teacher, and it is a stubborn one, because concrete is harder to repeal than a paragraph.

This lesson is double-edged. Good public works can widen opportunity: a library within walking distance, a sewer that ends a cholera season, a bridge that brings two labour markets together. Poor or unjust works can freeze a hierarchy: a red-lined district with fewer stations, a capital’s avenues designed for parades rather than for the poor who must cross them, a colonial railway that extracts crops and leaves little local industry. Later generations inherit both the gift and the trap. They may not even see the trap, because a route feels like nature once it is familiar. History suggests a habit of asking, of any grand project, who was at the table, who was moved, and who will still be paying, or benefiting, in fifty years.

The past also warns against the fantasy of a clean slate. Cities that tried to erase “outdated” streets sometimes destroyed communities that held knowledge no master plan contained. Conversely, refusal to repair an ageing system can be a quiet decision to let it fail on the backs of those who cannot leave. Maintenance is an unheroic historical force. Empires and companies have often preferred the ribbon on a new line to the dull work of keeping an old one safe. The bill arrives later, as a collapse, a flood, or a generation without decent trains.

Students can practise this way of seeing on a local map. Choose a station, a housing block, or a river wall, and find when it was built and for what announced purpose. Then ask what unexpected uses and harms followed. Compare a hopeful speech from the opening day, if one survives, with a later report. The gap is often where the real lesson lives. History’s insight is not that building is foolish. It is that building is a moral act stretched across time, and that humility about future users should be part of the design.

A society that remembers this will argue not only about the cost of a project in this year’s budget, but about the kind of life the project will make ordinary for people not yet born. The past is under our feet as well as in our books. If we learn to read a street as a document, we are less likely to be surprised when it goes on speaking after we have gone.
senior.translation:
一篇演说持续一天；一条路可以持续一个世纪。历史安静的教训之一是，基础设施——铁路、港口、运河、电线、住宅区、学校的地图——在它被开通的仪式过去很久之后，仍然继续塑造生活。一条偏爱某一个港口的铁路，可以使另一座城市缩小。一条切开街区的公路，可以把它分割好几代。一座大坝可以带来光，也可以淹没一座山谷的记忆。当我们问过去仍然有什么可以教时，人很容易只去看战争、法律和伟大的书。被建造出来的世界也是一位老师，而且是一位固执的老师，因为混凝土比一段文字更难废除。

这一课是双刃的。好的公共工程可以扩大机会：一座步行可及的图书馆，一条结束霍乱季节的下水道，一座把两个劳动力市场连在一起的桥。糟糕或不公正的工程可以冻结一种等级：一个车站更少的红线分区，一条为游行而不是为必须穿过它们的穷人设计的都城大道，一条抽取作物、却留下很少本地工业的殖民铁路。后来的世代既继承礼物，也继承陷阱。他们甚至可能看不见陷阱，因为一条路一旦熟悉，就感觉像自然。历史建议一种习惯：对任何宏大项目都问，谁曾坐在桌边，谁被移动了，以及五十年后谁仍将在支付，或在受益。

过去也警告那种干净石板的幻想。试图擦去“过时”街道的城市，有时摧毁了掌握着任何总规划都不包含的知识的社区。反过来，拒绝修理一个老化的系统，可能是一个安静的决定：让它在那些无法离开的人的背上失败。维护是一种非英雄的历史力量。帝国和公司常常更喜欢新线路上的彩带，而不是保持旧线路安全的乏味工作。账单稍后到来，以倒塌、洪水，或没有像样列车的一代人的形式。

学生可以在一张本地地图上练习这种看的方式。选一个车站、一栋住宅，或一道河堤，找出它何时被建造，以及宣布的目的是什么。然后问随后跟来了哪些意外的用途和伤害。如果还留得下一篇开通日的乐观演说，就把它和一份后来的报告比较。缝隙常常就是真正的教训居住的地方。历史的洞见不是建造是愚蠢的。而是建造是一种伸展在时间里的道德行为，而对未来使用者的谦逊，应当成为设计的一部分。

一个记得这一点的社会，将争论的不仅是一个项目在今年预算里的成本，还有这个项目将使尚未出生的人感到平常的那种生活。过去既在我们的脚下，也在我们的书里。如果我们学会把一条街当作一份文件来读，当它在我们走了之后仍继续说话时，我们就比较不容易吃惊。

questions.q: 1. Why does the passage call the built world a stubborn teacher?
options: Infrastructure can shape lives for a century, and concrete is harder to repeal than a paragraph, so a road, a dam or a rail keeps teaching after the opening ceremony
A speech lasts as long as a road, and only wars and great books have lessons
A highway cut through a neighbourhood never divides it for long
A railway that favours one port cannot make another city shrink
questions.exp: 文中说基础设施在开通仪式很久之后仍塑造生活，混凝土比一段文字更难废除。

questions.q: 2. How is the lesson double-edged?
options: Public works never widen opportunity or freeze a hierarchy
A red-lined district with fewer stations is only a gift
Familiar routes never hide a trap, because they are nature
Good works can widen opportunity, while unjust works can freeze a hierarchy, and later generations inherit both the gift and a trap that may start to feel like nature
questions.exp: 文中对比步行可及的图书馆、下水道和桥梁，与红线分区、游行大道和殖民铁路，后代既继承礼物也继承陷阱。

questions.q: 3. What questions should be asked of any grand project, according to history?
options: How can we guarantee a clean slate by erasing ‘outdated’ streets
Why maintenance should be ignored in favour of a ribbon on a new line
Who was at the table, who was moved, and who will still be paying or benefiting in fifty years
How to let an ageing system fail only on those who cannot leave, as a virtue
questions.exp: 文中建议问谁在桌边、谁被移动、五十年后谁仍在支付或受益。

questions.q: 4. Why is maintenance called an unheroic historical force?
options: Refusal to repair is never a decision with human costs
Empires and companies often prefer a new line’s ceremony to keeping an old one safe, and the bill arrives later as a collapse, a flood, or a generation without decent trains
Destroying communities that hold unplanned knowledge is always wise
A clean slate is history’s favourite reliable strategy
questions.exp: 文中说维护常常被新线路的彩带比下去，账单稍后以倒塌、洪水或没有像样列车的一代人到来。

questions.q: 5. What local exercise helps students read a street as a document?
options: Choose a station, block or river wall, find when and why it was built, ask what unexpected uses and harms followed, and compare an opening speech with a later report
Argue only about this year’s budget, never about the life the project will make ordinary for people not yet born
Assume the past lives only in books, not under our feet
Avoid the gap between a hopeful speech and a later report, where the lesson often lives
questions.exp: 文中建议选一个本地建造物，查建造时间与宣布目的，追问意外用途与伤害，并比较开通演说和后来的报告。

senior.title: 📂 Reading the Archive Against the Grain: Whose Voice Is Missing?
senior.content:
History is often presented as a complete story: a timeline, a set of famous names, a conclusion that feels inevitable. One of the most useful lessons the past offers is more unsettling. The records from which that story is built were never neutral. Official archives keep what offices needed, what victors saved, and what literate people could write. Letters from the powerful survive more often than the jokes of a kitchen, the song of a field, or the testimony of someone who was not asked. When we read only what was filed, we risk mistaking a quiet absence for proof that nothing else happened. Historical insight begins when we ask, of every source: who could speak here, who was silent, and who had the power to throw the paper away?

Reading against the grain does not mean inventing a past we prefer. It means looking at the edges of a document for what it did not mean to reveal: a complaint in the margin, a list of rations that implies hunger, a law that is repeated so often that it must have been widely broken. It means seeking other kinds of evidence — oral histories, objects, landscapes, family books, court cases brought by the poor — and treating them as seriously as a minister’s memoir. It also means noticing when a later textbook has smoothed a conflict into a single national tale. The past is not only missing voices by accident. It is sometimes missing them by design.

This lesson has a present tense. Museums, school curricula and national days still choose whom to honour and whom to leave in a footnote. A more honest public history does not require us to despise every official record. It requires us to put those records in conversation with the people they overlooked, and to admit uncertainty where the evidence is thin. Some recoveries are now possible because descendants have insisted, because film or a diary was found, or because historians learned to count what was never meant to be counted. Other recoveries will remain incomplete. Humility is part of the method.

Students can practise on a short official text — a school rule from a former decade, a founding speech, a newspaper’s front page — and write two lists: what the text wants them to believe, and what questions it leaves unasked about servants, women, migrants, or opponents. If a local museum is nearby, they can ask which objects were given by elites, and which lives are represented only as types. The skill is not cynicism. It is a trained suspicion of completeness.

The past still matters because it shaped the ground we walk on, and because its silences can be inherited as if they were facts. A society that learns to look for the missing voice is less easily captured by a tidy myth. History’s deepest advice may be this: do not confuse the archive with the world, and do not confuse the loudest surviving story with the only one that was lived.
senior.translation:
历史常常被呈现为一个完整的故事：一条时间线，一组著名的名字，一个感觉不可避免的结论。过去提供的最有用的教训之一，却更让人不安。那个故事所由之建成的记录，从来不是中立的。官方档案保存的，是衙门所需要的，胜利者所留下的，以及识字的人能够写下的。有权者的信件，比厨房里的笑话、田野里的歌，或一个未被询问的人的证词，更常存活下来。当我们只阅读被归档的东西时，我们就有风险把一种安静的缺席，误当作没有别的事情发生过的证据。历史的洞见，开始于我们对每一份材料提问：谁能在这里说话，谁是沉默的，以及谁有权力把那张纸扔掉？

逆纹阅读并不意味着发明一段我们更喜欢的过去。它意味着看着一份文件的边缘，寻找它并不打算揭示的东西：页边的一句抱怨，一份暗示饥饿的配给名单，一条被重复得如此之勤、以致它一定曾被广泛违反的法律。它意味着寻找其他种类的证据——口述史、物品、风景、家庭账本、穷人所提起的官司——并像对待一位部长的回忆录一样严肃地对待它们。它也意味着注意到，后来的课本何时把一场冲突抚平成一个单一的国家故事。过去不仅会偶然缺失一些声音。它有时是被设计成缺失它们的。

这一课有一个现在时。博物馆、学校课程和国庆日仍然在选择荣耀谁、把谁留在脚注里。一种更诚实的公共历史，并不要求我们鄙视每一份官方记录。它要求我们让那些记录与它们所忽视的人对话，并在证据稀薄的地方承认不确定。有些恢复现在是可能的，因为后代坚持了，因为胶片或一本日记被找到了，或因为历史学家学会去计数那些从未被打算计数的东西。其他恢复将仍然是不完整的。谦逊是这种方法的一部分。

学生可以在一份简短的官方文本上练习——从前十年的一条校规，一篇奠基演说，一张报纸的头版——并写下两份清单：文本希望他们相信什么，以及它留下了哪些关于仆人、妇女、移民或反对者的未问的问题。如果附近有一座本地博物馆，他们可以问哪些物品是由精英赠送的，哪些生命仅仅作为类型被代表。这种技能不是犬儒。它是一种被训练过的、对完整性的怀疑。

过去仍然重要，因为它塑造了我们行走的地面，也因为它的沉默可以被继承得仿佛它们就是事实。一个学会寻找缺失声音的社会，比较不容易被一个整洁的神话所俘获。历史最深的建议也许是：不要把档案与世界混淆，也不要把那条存活得最响的故事，与唯一被度过的故事混淆。

questions.q: 1. Why were historical records never a complete, neutral story?
options: A timeline of famous names is already the whole of what was lived
Archives keep what offices needed, victors saved and literate people could write, so a quiet absence is not proof that nothing else happened
Kitchen jokes and unasked testimony survive as often as letters from the powerful
Anyone could always throw official paper away, so silence never needs to be questioned
questions.exp: 文中说档案保存衙门所需、胜利者所留和识字者能写的，安静的缺席不等于无事发生。

questions.q: 2. What does reading against the grain involve, if it is not inventing a preferred past?
options: Looking at a document’s edges for unintended evidence, seeking oral histories, objects and cases brought by the poor, and noticing when a textbook has smoothed a conflict
Treating a minister’s memoir as the only serious source
Assuming missing voices are only accidental, never designed
Accepting every later national tale as complete
questions.exp: 文中建议看文件边缘的无意证据，寻找口述史、物品和穷人所提官司，并注意课本对冲突的抚平。

questions.q: 3. How does this lesson have a present tense?
options: We must despise every official record in order to be honest
Recoveries are never possible, even when descendants insist or a diary is found
Humility has no place in the method once a museum has chosen its honours
Museums, curricula and national days still choose whom to honour; a more honest public history puts official records in conversation with overlooked people and admits uncertainty
questions.exp: 文中指出博物馆和国庆日仍在选择荣耀谁，诚实的公共历史应让官方记录与被忽视的人对话。

questions.q: 4. What two lists can students write from a short official text?
options: Only what a local museum was given by elites, with no questions about lives represented as types
A cynical rejection of every school rule or founding speech
What the text wants them to believe, and what questions it leaves unasked about servants, women, migrants or opponents
A proof that suspicion of completeness cannot be trained
questions.exp: 文中建议写下文本希望人相信什么，以及关于仆人、妇女、移民或反对者哪些问题未被问及。

questions.q: 5. What deepest advice does the passage say history offers?
options: Inherit silences as if they were facts, because a tidy myth is easier to live with
Do not confuse the archive with the world, or the loudest surviving story with the only one that was lived
Trust only the loudest story, because it has survived
Treat the ground we walk on as unrelated to the past
questions.exp: 文中说不要把档案与世界混淆，也不要把最响的存活故事当作唯一被度过的故事。

senior.title: 🚶 The Fifteen-Minute Test: Can Daily Life Be Reached on Foot?
senior.content:
For much of the last century, many growing cities were organised around the car: wide roads, separate zones for housing, shops and offices, and a daily commute that could swallow two hours. A newer question in urban development is almost childishly simple, and hard to achieve: can a person reach school, food, care, a park and a modest job within about a fifteen-minute walk or cycle from home? The “fifteen-minute” idea is not a magic number. It is a test of whether a neighbourhood is a living unit or only a bedroom attached to a distant centre. Cities that fail the test produce traffic, loneliness in empty daytime streets, and a childhood spent being driven between errands.

Mixed uses are at the heart of the test. A street that holds apartments above a bakery, a clinic beside a library, and a small square for a market can support trips that do not begin with a key in an ignition. This is not nostalgia for a postcard. It requires rules that allow shops in residential blocks, housing near workplaces, and public transport that links the neighbourhood to the rest of the city for the journeys that cannot be short. It also requires care about price. If “walkable” becomes a luxury label, the people who would benefit most — those without cars, the elderly, children, low-paid workers — may be pushed out by rising rents, and the district becomes a lifestyle brand rather than a fairer pattern.

Critics raise real issues. Some jobs cannot sit on every corner; a port, a hospital campus or a factory has its own geography. Some residents fear noise, or the loss of parking, or a plan imposed from above. A serious programme answers with design, not with a slogan: night-time rules for bars, safe crossings, trees, and a process in which local voices can change a drawing. It also admits that a fifteen-minute map will not look the same in a dense old core and in a spread-out suburb; the principle is short access, not a copied skyline.

Urban development, at this scale, is about time as a public good. Minutes spent in a jammed car are minutes not spent with family, study or rest. Air and safety improve when many short trips leave the car. Local shops gain regular customers. The risk is that the idea is used only in brochures for new luxury blocks, while existing estates remain cut off from a grocery or a clinic.

Students can apply the test where they live. List the essential places of a week, time the walk, and mark what is missing — a safe crossing, a bench, an evening bus, a shop that sells fruit. Then ask who would need those things more than a healthy teenager does. A city that develops well does not only grow outward. It grows closer, so that ordinary life can be reached on foot by more than those who can already afford to live at the centre.
senior.translation:
在上一个世纪的许多时间里，不少正在生长的城市是围绕汽车来组织的：宽路，把住房、商店和办公室分开的分区，以及一次可以吞掉两小时的日常通勤。城市发展里一个更新的问题，几乎幼稚地简单，却很难实现：一个人能否从家步行或骑行大约十五分钟，就到达学校、食物、医疗、一座公园，和一份适度的工作？“十五分钟”的想法并不是一个魔法数字。它是一次测试：一个街区是一个活着的单元，还是仅仅一间连在遥远中心上的卧室。没有通过测试的城市，会产生交通，空荡荡的白天街道里的孤独，以及在差事之间被开车送达的童年。

混合用途是这次测试的核心。一条在面包店上盖着公寓、在图书馆旁有诊所、还有一小块供市场使用的方地的街，可以支持并不从点火钥匙开始的行程。这不是对一张明信片的怀旧。它需要允许住宅楼里有商店、工作地点附近有住房的规则，以及把这个街区与城市其余部分连接起来、以完成那些不能变短的旅程的公共交通。它也需要对价格保持小心。如果“可步行”变成一种奢侈标签，那些最会受益的人——没有车的人，老人，孩子，低薪工作者——也许会被上涨的租金推出去，而这个区域就变成一种生活方式的品牌，而不是一种更公平的模式。

批评者提出真实的问题。有些工作不能坐在每一个转角；一个港口、一座医院园区或一家工厂有它自己的地理。有些居民担心噪音，或停车位的失去，或一份从上而下强加的计划。一个严肃的方案用设计而不是口号来回答：酒吧的夜间规则，安全的过街，树木，以及一个本地声音可以改变图纸的过程。它也承认，十五分钟的地图在一个密集的老中心和一个铺开的郊区不会看起来一样；原则是短的到达，而不是一道被复制的天际线。

在这个尺度上，城市发展关乎作为公共益处的时间。花在堵塞汽车里的分钟，是没有花在家庭、学习或休息上的分钟。当许多短途离开汽车时，空气和安全会改善。本地商店会得到规律的顾客。风险是，这个想法只被用在新的豪华楼盘的手册里，而现有的住宅区仍然与一家杂货店或诊所切断。

学生可以在他们居住的地方应用这次测试。列出一周里必要的地点，给步行计时，并标出缺少什么——一处安全的过街，一张长凳，一班晚间的公共汽车，一家卖水果的店。然后再问，谁会比一个健康的青少年更需要那些东西。一座发展得好的城市，并不只是向外生长。它向更近处生长，好让普通生活能够被更多人步行到达，而不只是那些已经买得起住在中心的人。

questions.q: 1. What is the ‘fifteen-minute’ idea a test of, if it is not a magic number?
options: Whether every city must be organised around a two-hour car commute
Whether wide roads and separate zones always produce a living unit
Whether a neighbourhood is a living unit in which school, food, care, a park and a modest job can be reached on foot or by cycle, rather than only a bedroom attached to a distant centre
Whether children should spend childhood being driven between errands
questions.exp: 文中说十五分钟不是魔法数字，而是测试街区是活的单元还是连在遥远中心上的卧室。

questions.q: 2. Why must mixed uses be paired with care about price?
options: Shops in residential blocks and housing near workplaces are only nostalgia for a postcard
If ‘walkable’ becomes a luxury label, those without cars, the elderly, children and low-paid workers may be pushed out by rents, and the district becomes a brand rather than a fairer pattern
Public transport should not link the neighbourhood to longer journeys
Rising rents always protect the people who would benefit most
questions.exp: 文中警告若可步行成为奢侈标签，最需要的人可能被租金推走，街区变成生活方式品牌。

questions.q: 3. How should a serious programme answer critics who fear noise, lost parking or a plan from above?
options: With design and process: night-time rules, safe crossings, trees, and local voices that can change a drawing, plus an admission that a dense core and a suburb will not look the same
With a slogan, and a copied skyline for every suburb
By placing a port or a factory on every corner
By ignoring geography and imposing one map everywhere
questions.exp: 文中主张用夜间规则、安全过街、树木和可修改图纸的本地过程来回答，并承认老中心与郊区形态不同。

questions.q: 4. What risk appears if the idea is used only in brochures for luxury blocks?
options: Local shops never gain regular customers when short trips leave the car
Time spent in traffic is already a public good
Air and safety cannot improve when short trips leave the car
Existing estates may remain cut off from a grocery or a clinic, while minutes in jammed cars and poorer air continue for everyone else
questions.exp: 文中担心这个想法只出现在豪华楼盘手册里，而现有住宅区仍然远离杂货店或诊所。

questions.q: 5. How can students apply the test where they live?
options: Assume the city should only grow outward, never closer
Ignore benches, evening buses and safe crossings as extras
List the essential places of a week, time the walk, mark what is missing, and ask who would need those things more than a healthy teenager does
Design a city only for those who can already afford to live at the centre
questions.exp: 文中建议列出一周必要地点、给步行计时、标出缺失，并问谁比健康青少年更需要这些东西。

senior.title: 🌡️ Designing a City That Can Survive Its Own Heat
senior.content:
Cities are often warmer than the fields around them. Dark roofs and roads store the sun, air-conditioners pour heat into narrow streets, and a lack of trees leaves no shade for a bus stop at noon. As summers grow more intense, urban development can no longer treat heat as a weather report. It is a design problem that already sends people to hospital, reduces the ability to work outdoors, and makes some neighbourhoods less liveable than others — often the ones with less greenery and more exposed concrete. A serious city plan now asks not only where the next tower will stand, but where a person can walk at three in the afternoon without becoming ill.

Cooling is a set of ordinary materials and habits, not a single machine. Lighter surfaces reflect more of the sun; shade from trees, colonnades or simple canopies can drop the temperature of a pavement enough to change a journey; water in parks and fountains cools by evaporation, if it is not wasted. Buildings can be placed to keep a breeze, and windows can be designed so that night air is usable. Air-conditioning will remain necessary for many hospitals, schools and homes, but a city that relies on it alone pushes heat into the street and raises the power demand just when the grid is most strained. Equity matters here. A cooling centre is a poor substitute for a neighbourhood that was allowed, for decades, to become a heat island while richer streets kept their trees.

Development decisions lock these patterns in. A parking lot poured today will be a furnace in twenty years unless it is shaded or broken up. A wide, treeless avenue photographs well and punishes pedestrians. Informal additions of metal roofs can make rooms unbearable unless ventilation and insulation are part of upgrading, not an afterthought. Planners who only count floor space miss the public health of the street. Heat should sit beside traffic and housing in the same meeting, with data that show which blocks already suffer, and with money that reaches those blocks first.

Residents have knowledge that a map may lack: which wall is unlivable in August, which crossing has no shade for a pram, which night is too hot to sleep. Good urban development listens, then plants, paints, and rewrites a rule about a front setback or a parking requirement so that a tree has room to grow. Maintenance — watering a young tree, keeping a fountain on — is again the unheroic work that decides whether a plan survives its first dry season.

Students can walk a familiar route at the hottest hour and note surfaces, shade and places a vulnerable person would have to stop. They can compare a tree-lined street with a bare one a block away, and ask what rule or budget made the difference. A city that develops as if heat were optional will invent its own crisis. A city that designs for shade and night-time cooling is taking the next fifty summers as seriously as the next fifty towers.
senior.translation:
城市常常比周围的田更暖。深色的屋顶和道路储存太阳，空调把热倒进窄街，缺少树木则使中午的公交站没有荫凉。当夏天变得更强烈时，城市发展不能再把热当作一份天气预报。它是一个设计问题，已经把人送进医院，降低户外工作的能力，并使一些街区比另一些更不宜居——常常是那些绿化更少、暴露的混凝土更多的街区。一份严肃的城市计划现在不仅问下一座塔将站在哪里，也问一个人如何能在下午三点行走而不生病。

冷却是一套平常的材料和习惯，不是单单一台机器。更浅的表面反射更多阳光；树木、柱廊或简单的遮篷投下的荫凉，可以把人行道的温度降到足以改变一次旅程；公园和喷泉里的水通过蒸发来冷却，如果它不被浪费。建筑可以被放置来保留微风，窗户可以被设计成夜间的空气可用。对许多医院、学校和住宅来说，空调将仍然必要，但一座只依赖它的城市，会把热推到街上，并恰好在电网最紧张时提高电力需求。公平在这里很重要。一个降温中心，是对一个被允许在几十年里变成热岛、而更富的街道却留着树的街区的、很差的替代。

发展决定会把这些模式锁住。今天浇筑的一个停车场，除非被遮荫或被拆散，二十年后会是一座熔炉。一条宽阔、没有树的大道拍照好看，却惩罚行人。金属屋顶的非正式加建，可能使房间难以忍受，除非通风和隔热是升级的一部分，而不是事后想法。只计算楼面面积的规划者，会错过街道的公共卫生。热应当在同一次会议里，和交通、住房坐在一起，带着显示哪些街区已经在受苦的数据，以及先到达那些街区的资金。

居民拥有一张地图可能缺少的知识：哪一面墙在八月无法居住，哪一处过街没有给婴儿车的荫凉，哪一个夜晚热得无法睡觉。好的城市发展会倾听，然后种植、粉刷，并改写一条关于前院退让或停车要求的规则，好让一棵树有空间生长。维护——给一棵小树浇水，让一座喷泉开着——再次是那种决定一份计划能否度过第一个旱季的、非英雄的工作。

学生可以在最热的一小时走一条熟悉的路，并记下表面、荫凉，以及一个脆弱的人将不得不停下的地方。他们可以比较一条有树的街和一条街区之外光秃的街，并问是什么规则或预算造成了差别。一座把热当作可选项来发展的城市，会发明它自己的危机。一座为荫凉和夜间冷却而设计的城市，是在像对待未来五十座塔一样认真地对待未来的五十个夏天。

options: A person can always walk at three in the afternoon without becoming ill
Towers are the only question a serious plan should ask
Greenery and exposed concrete never differ between neighbourhoods
Cities are already warmer than surrounding fields, and heat sends people to hospital, reduces outdoor work and makes some, often greener-poor, neighbourhoods less liveable

questions.q: 2. Which ordinary cooling methods does the passage name besides air-conditioning?
options: Relying on air-conditioning alone, which never pours heat into the street
A cooling centre as a full substitute for trees on richer streets
Lighter surfaces, shade from trees or canopies, water that cools by evaporation, breezes between buildings, and windows that can use night air
Wasting fountain water, which is the main method
questions.exp: 文中列举浅色表面、树与遮篷的荫凉、蒸发冷却、保留微风和可用的夜间空气。

questions.q: 3. How do today’s development decisions lock in future heat?
options: Heat should stay out of meetings about traffic and housing
A parking lot poured now can be a furnace in twenty years, a treeless avenue punishes pedestrians, and metal roofs can make rooms unbearable without ventilation and insulation
Money should reach the coolest blocks first, and data on suffering blocks are unnecessary
Planners who only count floor space already capture the public health of the street

questions.q: 4. What knowledge can residents add to a map?
options: Which wall is unlivable in August, which crossing has no shade for a pram, and which night is too hot to sleep — knowledge that should lead to planting, paint and rules that give a tree room
A map already contains every August wall and sleepless night
Watering a young tree is unrelated to whether a plan survives a dry season
Front setbacks and parking rules should never be rewritten for a tree

questions.q: 5. What walking exercise can students do at the hottest hour?
options: Treat heat as optional, so the city can invent its own crisis
Ignore rules and budgets that made the difference between two streets
Take the next fifty towers seriously, and the next fifty summers not at all
Note surfaces, shade and places a vulnerable person would have to stop, and compare a tree-lined street with a bare one a block away
questions.exp: 文中建议在最热的一小时记录表面与荫凉，并比较有树的街和一条之外光秃的街。

senior.title: 🔗 Elaboration: Connecting New Ideas to What You Already Know
senior.content:
A student can copy a definition, highlight a paragraph, and still be unable to use the idea the next day. One reason is that the new sentence has nowhere to sit. Elaboration is a study strategy that gives it a seat: you explain the idea in your own words, connect it to something you already understand, and ask how it would change if a condition changed. Cognitive research has long suggested that knowledge which is linked to existing schemas is easier to retrieve later than knowledge that was only repeated. The method is slower than rereading, and that slowness is the point. You are not decorating the page. You are building a path that your future self can walk.

The practice can be modest and still rigorous. After a short section, close the book and say, or write, “This is basically…, which is like…, and it matters because…” If you cannot finish the sentence, you have found the edge of your understanding, which is more useful than a page of yellow ink. A physics idea can be linked to a bicycle; a historical cause can be linked to a family story, provided you also notice where the analogy fails. A good elaboration includes a limit: “This is like X, except that…” That exception keeps the new idea from dissolving into a vague familiarity. Teachers who ask “why might this be true?” or “what would happen if…?” are already training the same muscle.

There are traps. Elaboration is not the same as inventing a long, pretty example that hides a gap, or as telling a story so freely that the original meaning disappears. If the connection is wrong, it can be worse than no connection, because a vivid error travels well. Checking the link against the text, a worked example, or a classmate’s version is part of the strategy. Nor should elaboration replace all other work. You still need practice in using the idea on new problems. The elaboration makes that practice more efficient, because you know what you are looking for.

Students can keep a narrow notebook for this purpose: one idea, two connections, one “what if,” and a mark of whether the explanation still made sense the next day. In a group, each person can offer a different link, then the group can vote on which links are accurate and which are only charming. Over a term, the notebook becomes a map of how your mind actually holds the course, not only of what the syllabus listed.

A learning strategy is only as good as the situation it fits. Elaboration shines when the material has meaning to unpack, and it helps less when the task is a pure motor skill or a list that must simply be available. Used in the right place, it turns study from a hope that familiarity will become knowledge into a deliberate act of weaving. What you already know is not a distraction from school. It is the hook on which new thought can hang.
senior.translation:
一个学生可以抄下一个定义，给一段文字涂上高亮，第二天却仍然不会使用这个想法。一个原因是，那句新话没有地方可坐。精加工是一种给它一个座位的学习策略：你用自己的话解释这个想法，把它连接到你已经理解的某件事上，并问如果一个条件改变，它会怎样变化。认知研究长期以来提示，连接到已有图式上的知识，比仅仅被重复的知识，稍后更容易被提取。这种方法比重读更慢，而那种慢正是重点。你不是在装饰页面。你是在建造一条未来的自己可以走的路。

这种练习可以是谦逊的，却仍然严谨。在一小段之后，合上书，说或写下：“这基本上是……，它像……，而它重要是因为……”如果你不能完成这个句子，你就找到了理解的边缘，这比一页黄色墨水更有用。一个物理想法可以连接到一辆自行车；一个历史原因可以连接到一个家庭故事，只要你也注意到类比在何处失效。一次好的精加工包括一个限度：“这像X，只不过……”那个例外，能防止新想法溶解成一种模糊的熟悉。那些问“这为什么可能是真的？”或“如果……会怎样？”的老师，已经在训练同一块肌肉。

也有陷阱。精加工并不等于发明一个又长又漂亮、却藏着缺口的例子，或把故事讲得如此自由，以致原来的意思消失。如果连接是错的，它可能比没有连接更糟，因为一个生动的错误传得很好。对照文本、一道已解的例题，或同学的版本来检查这条链接，是这种策略的一部分。精加工也不应当代替所有其他工作。你仍然需要在新问题上使用这个想法的练习。精加工使那种练习更有效，因为你知道自己在寻找什么。

学生可以为这个目的保留一本狭窄的笔记本：一个想法，两个连接，一个“如果……会怎样”，以及一个关于第二天这个解释是否仍然说得通的记号。在小组里，每个人可以提供一条不同的链接，然后小组可以投票，哪些链接是准确的，哪些只是讨人喜欢。在一个学期里，这本笔记本会变成一张关于你的头脑实际上如何握住这门课的地图，而不仅仅是教学大纲列出了什么。

一种学习策略，只有在适合它的情境里才好。当材料有可以打开的意义时，精加工会发光；当任务只是一种纯粹的动作技能，或一份必须简单可用的清单时，它的帮助就更少。用在恰当的地方，它会把学习从一种“熟悉将会变成知识”的希望，变成一种有意的编织。你已经知道的东西，并不是对学校的干扰。它是新思想可以挂上去的钩子。

questions.q: 1. What is elaboration as a study strategy, according to the passage?
options: Explaining an idea in your own words, connecting it to something you already understand, and asking how it would change if a condition changed
Copying a definition and highlighting a paragraph until familiarity becomes knowledge
Rereading as quickly as possible, because slowness is a waste
Decorating the page so that the new sentence has nowhere to sit
questions.exp: 文中把精加工定义为用自己的话解释、连接到已有理解，并追问条件改变时会怎样。

questions.q: 2. Why can a sentence such as ‘This is like X, except that…’ improve the strategy?
options: Every analogy should be told so freely that the original meaning disappears
A bicycle or a family story should be linked without noticing any limit
Yellow ink is a more useful sign of the edge of understanding than an unfinished sentence
The exception keeps the new idea from dissolving into a vague familiarity, and it shows where an analogy fails
questions.exp: 文中强调好的精加工包含限度，以免新想法溶成模糊的熟悉，并标明类比失效之处。

questions.q: 3. What trap does the writer warn against?
options: Elaboration should replace all practice on new problems
Inventing a long, pretty example that hides a gap is the best form of the method
A vivid but wrong connection can travel well and be worse than no connection, so the link should be checked against the text, an example, or a classmate
Checking a link is unnecessary once the story feels charming
questions.exp: 文中警告错误却生动的连接可能比没有连接更糟，需要对照文本、例题或同学来检查。

questions.q: 4. What can students keep in a narrow notebook for this purpose?
options: Only the syllabus list, with no map of how the mind holds the course
One idea, two connections, one ‘what if,’ and a later mark of whether the explanation still made sense the next day
A group vote on which links are charming, with no interest in accuracy
A record that never returns the next day
questions.exp: 文中建议一本窄笔记本：一个想法、两个连接、一个如果、以及次日是否仍说得通的记号。

questions.q: 5. When does elaboration shine, and when does it help less?
options: It shines when the material has meaning to unpack, and helps less for a pure motor skill or a list that must simply be available
It is equally perfect for every motor skill and every meaningful idea
What you already know is only a distraction from school and should not be used as a hook
The strategy never needs to fit the situation
questions.exp: 文中说当材料有可展开的意义时精加工最有效，对纯动作技能或只需备用的清单帮助较少。

senior.title: 🖊️ Self-Explanation: Talking Through a Problem as You Solve It
senior.content:
Many students watch a worked example, nod, and then stall when the numbers change. The example felt clear because someone else’s thinking was already on the page. Self-explanation is a strategy for making that thinking your own: as you solve, or as you study a model answer, you say — quietly, in writing, or in your head — why each step is there, what rule it uses, and what you would try if the step failed. Research on learning has found that students who explain the steps to themselves often outperform those who only reread the solution, even when the total time is similar. The voice in the margin is doing work that highlighting cannot do. It is turning a sequence of lines into a set of decisions.

The method is most powerful when it is specific. “I get it” is not an explanation. “I divided by four because the area was split into equal parts” is. So is “I almost used the first formula, but the units are rates, so I need the second.” When you study a completed proof or a model essay, cover the next line and predict it, then compare; the mismatch is information. When you are stuck, narrating the stall — “I know the start and the goal, but I cannot see how this given fact helps” — often reveals a smaller question you can actually ask a teacher or a book. Self-explanation is not a performance of confidence. It is a flashlight pointed at the joint between what you know and what you are doing.

There are ways to misuse it. Talking at length without checking the result can fix an error in place. A silent, accurate check, or a comparison with the key, should follow the talk. Some students also turn the strategy into a script they recite without looking at the new problem’s details; the point is to explain this problem, not a generic one. In a noisy room the “talk” can be a few written phrases in the margin. In a pair, one student can solve while thinking aloud, and the other can ask “why that?” without taking over the pencil. The goal is ownership, not a second lecture.

Teachers can leave a little space beside solutions for these phrases, and can model one self-explanation in class so that the habit has a sound. Students can choose three problems, not thirty, and do them this way, then try one in silence to see whether the decisions still appear. Over weeks, the inner voice becomes shorter and more precise, which is a sign of growing skill, not of laziness.

A learning strategy earns its keep when it changes what you can do alone at a desk. Self-explanation is a way of refusing to be a spectator of your own work. If you can say why a step is there, you are more likely to find a cousin step when the problem is dressed in new clothes. That is not magic. It is practice at making thinking visible, so that it can be improved.
senior.translation:
许多学生看一道已解的例题，点头，然后当数字改变时就卡住。例子感觉清楚，是因为别人的思考已经在纸上了。自我解释是一种让那种思考成为你自己的策略：在你解题时，或在你研究一份模范答案时，你说出——轻轻地、写下来，或在心里——每一步为什么在那里，它使用了什么规则，以及如果这一步失败你将尝试什么。关于学习的研究发现，对自己解释步骤的学生，常常比只重读解答的学生表现更好，即使总时间相似。页边的那个声音，在做高亮所不能做的工作。它把一串行变成一组决定。

这种方法在具体时最有力量。“我懂了”不是一种解释。“我除以四，是因为面积被分成了相等的部分”才是。同样，“我几乎用了第一个公式，但单位是比率，所以我需要第二个。”当你研究一份完成的证明或一篇范文时，盖住下一行并预测它，然后再比较；不匹配就是信息。当你卡住时，叙述这次停顿——“我知道开头和目标，却看不出这个已知事实如何帮忙”——常常会揭示出一个你真正可以向老师或书本提出的更小的问题。自我解释不是一场关于自信的表演。它是一支照向你所知道的和你正在做的之间那个接头的手电筒。

也有误用它的方式。长篇大论却不检查结果，可能把一个错误固定下来。在说话之后，应当跟上一次安静而准确的核对，或与答案的比较。有些学生也会把这种策略变成一套他们背诵的脚本，却不看新问题的细节；重点是解释这一道题，而不是一道通用的题。在嘈杂的房间里，“说”可以是页边的几个写下来的短语。在两人一组时，一个学生可以一边解题一边出声思考，另一个可以问“为什么是那样？”而不把铅笔拿走。目标是所有权，不是第二场讲座。

老师可以在解答旁边留下一点空间给这些短语，并可以在课堂上示范一次自我解释，好让这个习惯有一种声音。学生可以选择三道题，而不是三十道，用这种方式来做，然后再在安静中试一道，看那些决定是否仍然出现。几周之后，内在的声音会变得更短、更精确，这是技能在生长的标志，而不是懒惰。

一种学习策略，在它改变了你独自坐在桌边能够做的事情时，才赚回了自己的位置。自我解释是一种拒绝成为自己工作的旁观者的方式。如果你能说出一步为什么在那里，当问题穿着新衣服时，你就更可能找到一个表亲的步骤。那不是魔法。它是让思考变得可见、好让它能够被改进的练习。

questions.q: 1. Why can a worked example feel clear and then fail when the numbers change?
options: Because highlighting already turns a sequence of lines into a set of decisions
Because someone else’s thinking was already on the page, whereas self-explanation makes each step’s reason and fallback your own
Because rereading a solution always outperforms explaining the steps
Because ‘I get it’ is already a complete explanation
questions.exp: 文中说例题感觉清楚是因为别人的思考已在纸上，自我解释是把每一步的理由变成自己的。

questions.q: 2. Which kind of sentence counts as a real self-explanation?
options: A specific reason, such as dividing because the area was split into equal parts, or rejecting a formula because the units are rates
A long talk that never checks the result
A generic script recited without looking at this problem’s details
A silent nod, with no prediction of the next line of a proof
questions.exp: 文中举例“因为面积被等分所以除以四”，或因单位是比率而改用第二个公式。

questions.q: 3. What should follow the talking, so that an error is not fixed in place?
options: A second lecture from the partner, who takes the pencil
No check at all, so that ownership is delayed
Only a performance of confidence, with no flashlight on the stall
A silent, accurate check or a comparison with the key, and, in a pair, a ‘why that?’ that does not take over the pencil
questions.exp: 文中说说话之后应有安静准确的核对或与答案比较；同伴可问为什么但不拿走铅笔。

questions.q: 4. How can students start without doing thirty problems this way?
options: Do thirty problems with a long script and no later silent test
Avoid any model of the habit in class, so that it has no sound
Choose three problems, use the method, then try one in silence to see whether the decisions still appear; over weeks the inner voice should become shorter and more precise
Treat a shorter inner voice as laziness rather than growing skill
questions.exp: 文中建议先做三道，再在安静中试一道；几周后内在声音更短更精确，是技能生长而非懒惰。

questions.q: 5. Why does the writer say self-explanation is not magic?
options: It allows you to remain a spectator of your own work at a desk
It is practice at making thinking visible so it can be improved, which helps you find a cousin step when a problem is dressed in new clothes
It replaces all decisions with highlighting
It works only when you never say why a step is there
questions.exp: 文中说这不是魔法，而是让思考可见以便改进的练习，从而在题目换装时更能找到表亲步骤。

senior.title: ⚖️ Environmental Justice: Why Some Neighbourhoods Breathe Worse Air
senior.content:
Discussions of environmental ethics often travel to distant forests or to future centuries. A harder question sits closer to home: why do some neighbourhoods, often poorer or home to minority communities, live with worse air, louder roads, fewer trees, and a higher chance of a dump, a plant, or a flood? Environmental justice is the claim that the benefits and the burdens of industrial life should not be distributed as if some lives were cheaper. It is not a substitute for caring about species or climate. It is the insistence that a clean river and a safe schoolyard are also moral goods, and that a policy which improves a city’s average while leaving one street to choke has not yet met an ethical test.

The pattern is not a coincidence of weather. Historically, factories, highways and waste sites were placed where land was cheap and political voice was weak. Once they are there, property values fall, and the next unwanted facility follows the same path. Health data, in many cities, still show higher rates of asthma and heat illness in these districts. The ethical issue is not only past placement. It is present decision: who is invited to the meeting about a new warehouse, whose traffic counts, and whether “no one lives there” is allowed to mean “no one who will be heard lives there.” A community that must organise for years merely to get a monitor for the air is already paying a tax that a leafier district does not pay.

Justice in this field has several tools, and none is only a speech. It can mean stricter rules on what may be built near homes and schools, real power to refuse or redesign a project, funds that clean the worst sites first, and health services that do not wait for a citywide average to look acceptable. It can mean planting and cooling in the hottest streets, not only in parks that already photograph well. It also means data that are public and local, so that a smell at night can become a measurement, not a rumour that officials can dismiss. Compensation, if it comes, should not be a quiet payment that buys silence while the harm continues.

There are tensions. A city needs goods, jobs and vehicles; not every plant can be wished away. Workers in a polluting industry may live in the same neighbourhood and fear unemployment more than a distant risk. Honest ethics holds both facts and still refuses to treat one community as the city’s sacrifice zone. Alternatives — cleaner technology, rerouted trucks, buffers of trees, relocation of the most dangerous processes — are design questions with moral weight, not luxuries.

Students can map a local contrast: two districts, their trees, their traffic, their distance to a park or a chimney, and ask who decided. Environmental ethics that never walks these streets can become an abstraction. Justice begins when the right to breathe, to sleep, and to keep children outdoors is treated as a shared right, not as a privilege of postcode.
senior.translation:
关于环境伦理的讨论，常常走向遥远的森林或未来的世纪。一个更难的问题坐得更近：为什么一些街区，常常更穷，或是少数群体的家，会与更糟的空气、更吵的道路、更少的树，以及更高的垃圾场、工厂或洪水的机会生活在一起？环境公正是这样一种主张：工业生活的益处和负担，不应当被分配得仿佛有些生命更便宜。它不是对物种或气候的关心的替代。它是一种坚持：一条干净的河和一个安全的校园也是道德上的益处，而一项改善一座城市的平均数、却留下一条街去窒息的政策，还没有通过伦理的测试。

这种模式并不是天气的巧合。在历史上，工厂、公路和废物场地被放在土地便宜、政治声音软弱的地方。一旦它们在那里，地产价值就会下降，下一个不受欢迎的设施就会走同一条路。在许多城市里，健康数据仍然显示这些区域有更高的哮喘和热病发生率。伦理问题不仅仅是过去的选址。它是现在的决定：谁被邀请参加关于一座新仓库的会议，谁的车流被计算，以及“那里没人住”是否被允许意味着“那里没有将被听见的人住。”一个必须组织多年、仅仅为了得到一台空气监测器的社区，已经在支付一个树更多的区域并不支付的税。

这个领域里的公正有几种工具，没有一种只是演说。它可以意味着对住宅和学校附近可以建造什么有更严的规则，拒绝或重新设计一个项目的真正权力，先清洁最糟地点的资金，以及不等待全市平均数看起来可接受的健康服务。它可以意味着在最热的街道上种植和降温，而不仅仅在已经很好拍照的公园里。它也意味着公开而本地的数据，好让夜里的一种气味可以变成一种测量，而不是官员可以驳回的谣言。如果有补偿，它不应当是一种买来沉默、却让伤害继续的安静付款。

这里有张力。一座城市需要货物、工作和车辆；不是每一座工厂都可以被愿望掉。污染行业里的工人可能住在同一街区，并且对失业的恐惧超过对一种遥远风险的恐惧。诚实的伦理握住这两个事实，却仍然拒绝把一个社区当作城市的牺牲区。替代方案——更清洁的技术，改道的卡车，树木的缓冲，最危险流程的迁移——是带有道德重量的设计问题，而不是奢侈。

学生可以画一幅本地的对比：两个区域，它们的树，它们的车流，它们离公园或烟囱的距离，并问是谁决定的。从不走过这些街道的环境伦理，可能变成一种抽象。公正开始于把呼吸、睡眠和让孩子留在户外的权利，当作一种共享的权利，而不是一种邮编的特权。

questions.q: 1. What claim does environmental justice make in this passage?
options: Caring about species or climate should replace any concern for a schoolyard or a river
Worse air in some neighbourhoods is only a coincidence of weather
The benefits and burdens of industrial life should not be distributed as if some lives were cheaper, and a citywide average that leaves one street to choke has not yet met an ethical test
A clean river is not a moral good compared with a future century

questions.q: 2. Why is the pattern described as historical and political, not only environmental?
options: No one is ever left out of a meeting about a new warehouse

Factories, highways and waste sites were often placed where land was cheap and voice was weak, then values fell and the next facility followed, while some communities must organise for years just to get an air monitor
‘No one lives there’ never means ‘no one who will be heard’
Leafier districts pay the same unofficial tax to get basic monitoring

questions.q: 3. Which tools of justice does the writer name besides speeches?
options: Stricter rules near homes and schools, power to refuse or redesign, funds that clean the worst sites first, cooling on the hottest streets, and public local data
A quiet payment that buys silence while the harm continues
Waiting until a citywide average looks acceptable before offering health services

options: Wish every plant away, with no design alternatives
Treat alternatives such as cleaner technology as luxuries without moral weight
Ignore workers’ fear and also accept a sacrifice zone
Admit that a city needs goods and that workers may fear unemployment, and still refuse to treat one community as a sacrifice zone, turning to cleaner technology, rerouted trucks or buffers

questions.q: 5. What local contrast can students map?
options: An abstract theory that never walks the streets
A single citywide average, with no contrast between neighbourhoods
Two districts’ trees, traffic, and distance to a park or a chimney, then ask who decided, so that the right to breathe is not treated as a privilege of postcode
A proof that keeping children outdoors is only a postcode privilege, never a shared right
questions.exp: 文中建议对比两个区域的树、车流和与公园或烟囱的距离，并追问是谁决定的。

senior.title: 💸 Carbon Offsets: Paying to Clean a Conscience, or a Real Repair?
senior.content:
A company, a flight, or even a concert can now be advertised as “carbon neutral.” The usual method is not to stop the emissions at the source, but to buy an offset: money paid so that trees will be planted, a forest will be protected, or a clean stove will be given to a household far away. In theory, a tonne of carbon kept out of the air in one place can cancel a tonne released in another. In ethics, the question is harder. When is an offset a genuine repair of harm, and when is it a receipt that lets a comfortable life continue unchanged? The answer matters, because a tool that soothes without reducing the original harm can delay the work that actually counts.

A serious offset has several conditions. The reduction must be real and measurable, not a hope written on a brochure. It must be additional: it would not have happened anyway, so the money is not paying for a forest that was already safe. It must last long enough; a tree that burns in ten years does not cancel a jet fuel that is still in the sky. It must not simply move the harm next door, and it should not be counted twice by two buyers. These tests are technical, and they are also moral, because they ask whether the claim of neutrality is honest. Investigations have found that some popular projects fail one or more of them. When they fail, the buyer has purchased a story, not a balance.

Even a high-quality offset leaves an ethical remainder. The people who live with a new plantation, or who lose access to land “protected” for carbon, are not a rounding error. Consent, fair payment, and a say in how the land is used belong in the design, not as an afterthought. There is also a question of symmetry. A wealthy flyer who offsets a holiday is not in the same position as a community that never flew and now hosts the trees. Offsetting can be a form of care if it is additional and just; it can also be a way of exporting a problem while keeping a lifestyle. Ethics asks who benefits from the comfort, and who carries the project.

A more demanding rule is order: reduce first, then offset what cannot yet be avoided, and say so clearly. A university, a city, or a family can cut wasted energy, change travel habits, and only then buy verified credits for the rest, without calling the whole life “neutral” as if the cut were optional. Students can read the fine print of a “green” ticket and ask three questions: what project, what proof of additionality, and what would have been done if the offset were unavailable? If the honest answer is “nothing would change,” the receipt is doing most of the moral work, and that is a warning.

Carbon mathematics will remain part of climate policy. The ethical task is to keep the mathematics from becoming a spell. Paying can be part of a repair. It should not be a licence to look away from the chimney that is still yours.
senior.translation:
一家公司、一次航班，甚至一场音乐会，现在都可以被宣传为“碳中和”。通常的方法并不是在源头停止排放，而是购买一种补偿：付钱，好让树被种下，一片森林被保护，或一个清洁炉灶被送给远方的一户人家。在理论上，在一个地方被挡在空气之外的一吨碳，可以抵消在另一个地方被放出的一吨。在伦理上，问题更难。什么时候一种补偿是对伤害的真正修复，什么时候它是一张让舒适生活继续不变的收据？这个答案很重要，因为一种只安抚、却不减少原来伤害的工具，会推迟真正算数的工作。

一次严肃的补偿有几个条件。减排必须是真实且可测量的，而不是写在小册子上的希望。它必须是额外的：它本来不会发生，所以这笔钱不是在为一片已经安全的森林付钱。它必须持续得足够久；一棵十年后烧掉的树，并不能抵消仍在天空中的航空燃料。它不应当只是把伤害挪到隔壁，也不应当被两个买家重复计算。这些测试是技术性的，它们也是道德的，因为它们在问中和的主张是否诚实。调查已经发现，一些受欢迎的项目未能通过其中一项或几项。当它们失败时，买家买到的是一个故事，而不是一种平衡。

即使是高质量的补偿，也留下一种伦理上的剩余。那些与一片新的种植园生活在一起的人，或那些失去对“为碳而保护”的土地的通路的人，并不是一个四舍五入的误差。同意、公平的付款，以及在土地如何被使用上的发言权，应当属于设计，而不是事后的想法。还有一个对称的问题。一个用补偿来抵消假期的富裕飞客，与一个从未飞过、现在却接待这些树的社区，并不处于同一位置。如果补偿是额外的且公正的，它可以是一种照料的形式；它也可以是一种在保持生活方式的同时把问题输出的方式。伦理会问，谁从舒适中受益，谁承担这个项目。

一条更苛求的规则是顺序：先减少，然后再补偿还不能避免的部分，并清楚地说出来。一所大学、一座城市，或一个家庭，可以削减被浪费的能源，改变出行习惯，然后才为其余部分购买经过核实的信用，而不把整个生活称为“中和”，仿佛削减是可选的。学生可以阅读一张“绿色”票的细则，并问三个问题：什么项目，额外性的什么证据，以及如果没有补偿本来会做什么？如果诚实的答案是“什么都不会改变”，那么这张收据就在做大部分的道德工作，而这是一个警告。

碳的数学仍将是气候政策的一部分。伦理的任务，是让这种数学不要变成一种咒语。付钱可以是修复的一部分。它不应当是一张让你从仍属于你的烟囱上移开目光的许可证。

questions.q: 1. What ethical question does the passage raise about carbon offsets?
options: Whether every concert must stop all emissions at the source before any tree is planted
Whether a tonne of carbon in one place can never, even in theory, be compared with a tonne in another
Whether mathematics should replace all climate policy
When an offset is a genuine repair of harm, and when it is a receipt that lets a comfortable life continue unchanged
questions.exp: 文中提出的伦理问题是：补偿何时是真正修复，何时只是让舒适生活不变的收据。

questions.q: 2. Which conditions make an offset serious, according to the writer?
options: A hope written on a brochure is enough if the project is popular
A tree that burns in ten years still cancels jet fuel in the sky
The reduction must be real, additional, lasting, not merely moved next door, and not counted twice
Paying for a forest that was already safe still counts as additional
questions.exp: 文中要求减排真实可测、具有额外性、足够持久、不把伤害挪到隔壁，且不被重复计算。

questions.q: 3. What ethical remainder remains even if an offset is high quality?
options: The host community is only a rounding error
People who live with a plantation or lose access to land need consent, fair payment and a say; a wealthy flyer is not in the same position as a host community
Exporting a problem while keeping a lifestyle has no ethical cost
Who benefits from the comfort never needs to be asked
questions.exp: 文中指出即使高质量补偿也涉及当地人的同意、公平付款和发言权，以及飞客与接待社区位置不对称。

questions.q: 4. What order does the writer call a more demanding rule?
options: Reduce first, then offset what cannot yet be avoided, and say so clearly, without calling a barely changed life ‘neutral’
Buy credits first, and treat cutting wasted energy as optional
Call the whole life carbon neutral as soon as a ticket is green
Avoid reading the fine print of a green ticket

questions.q: 5. What three questions can students ask of a ‘green’ ticket?
options: Only the price of the receipt, with no interest in the project
Whether mathematics has become a spell, with no other details
Whether paying can never be part of a repair
What project, what proof of additionality, and what would have been done if the offset were unavailable

senior.title: 🔧 Repair Cafés: Fixing Things Together Instead of Throwing Them Away
senior.content:
A toaster stops heating, a chair loses a leg, a phone screen cracks, and the usual next step is a bag for the bin or a click for a replacement. Repair cafés offer another next step: a regular table, often in a library, a church hall or a community centre, where people bring broken objects and sit with volunteer fixers who have tools, spare parts, and patience. The visitor usually keeps the object and does part of the work, so the skill moves, not only the object. The environmental gain is direct. An item that is used longer does not need to be manufactured again, and it does not arrive so soon in a landfill or a shipping container of waste. The social gain is quieter and also real: strangers talk, older knowledge is respected, and a neighbourhood practises a habit that shops of disposable goods do not teach.

Running such a space is itself a form of environmental action, because it changes what a community can do without waiting for a new law. Organisers find a room, insurance, a schedule, and a way to collect screws, fabric and chargers that would otherwise be thrown out. They post what can be attempted — lamps, bikes, clothes, small electronics — and what cannot, for safety. They teach one joint or one seam, then stand back. A successful afternoon is not measured only in items saved. It is measured in people who leave saying, “I could try this at home next time.” That sentence is a small transfer of power, away from a culture that treats every fault as a reason to buy.

The limits should be named honestly. Some devices are glued shut, parts are withheld, or a repair would cost more than a new unit priced to be temporary. A café cannot fix a law, and it should not pretend that volunteer evenings replace the right to repair, better design, or safer recycling of what cannot be saved. There is also a question of who comes. If the table is only convenient for people with spare Saturday hours and a car, the action misses those who most need a cheaper fix. Locating the café on a bus line, offering language help, and inviting young people as apprentices can widen the circle.

Schools and student groups can host a smaller version: a lunch-hour sewing and soldering table, a box of recovered parts, and a rule that a broken school item is tried before it is replaced. Cities can help with a room and a small budget for tools, without turning the café into a branding exercise. The work remains local and slightly imperfect, which is part of its honesty.

Environmental action is often imagined as a protest or a grand plan. Repair cafés show a third path: a repeated, practical gathering that keeps matter in use and keeps skill in circulation. A mended kettle will not by itself cool the planet. A street that knows how to mend, and that expects objects to last, is already living a different economy, one afternoon at a time.
senior.translation:
一台烤面包器停止加热，一把椅子掉了一条腿，一块手机屏幕裂了，通常的下一步是一只通向垃圾桶的袋子，或一次购买替代品的点击。维修咖啡馆提供另一种下一步：一张定期的桌子，常常在图书馆、教堂大厅或社区中心，人们把损坏的物品带来，与带着工具、备用零件和耐心的志愿修理者坐在一起。来访者通常保留物品，并做一部分工作，所以技能在移动，而不仅仅是物品。环境上的收益是直接的。一件被用得更久的物品，不需要再次被制造，也不会那么快到达填埋场或一箱废品的集装箱。社会上的收益更安静，也是真实的：陌生人交谈，更老的知识受到尊重，一个街区练习一种一次性商品的商店并不教授的习惯。

开办这样的空间本身就是一种环境行动，因为它改变了一个社区在不等待新法律的情况下能够做的事。组织者找到房间、保险、一个时间表，以及一种收集否则会被扔掉的螺丝、布料和充电器的方式。他们公布什么可以被尝试——灯、自行车、衣服、小电器——以及出于安全什么不可以。他们教一个接头或一道缝，然后退到一边。一个成功的下午，不仅仅用被救下的物品来衡量。它用离开时说“下次我可以在家里试试这个”的人来衡量。那句话是一次小小的权力转移，离开一种把每一个故障都当作购买理由的文化。

限度应当被诚实地说出。有些装置被胶死，零件被扣留，或一次修理会比一个被定价为暂时的新单位更贵。咖啡馆不能修理一部法律，也不应当假装志愿的晚上可以代替维修权、更好的设计，或对无法被挽救之物更安全的回收。还有一个谁会来的问题。如果这张桌子只对有空闲周六时间和一辆车的人方便，这种行动就会错过那些最需要更便宜修理的人。把咖啡馆放在公交线上，提供语言帮助，并邀请年轻人做学徒，可以扩大这个圈子。

学校和学生团体可以主办一个更小的版本：一张午餐时间的缝纫和焊接桌，一盒回收的零件，以及一条规则：一件损坏的学校物品在被替换之前先被尝试。城市可以帮忙提供房间和一小笔工具预算，而不把咖啡馆变成一次品牌练习。这项工作仍然是本地的，并且稍有不完美，而这正是它的诚实的一部分。

环境行动常常被想象为一次抗议或一个宏大的计划。维修咖啡馆显示了第三条路：一种反复的、实际的聚会，让物质保持在使用中，让技能保持在流通中。一把被修好的水壶不会独自冷却地球。一条知道如何修理、并期望物品持久的街道，已经在一个下午一个下午地，过着一种不同的经济。
